subsubtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Veterans Affairs says that there have not been any cuts to the Veterans Independence Program, yet the department itself is saying that it will save $9 million a year by cutting out heavy house cleaning for veterans.
There were only 19,000 veterans in 1989 who applied for any kind of housekeeping assistance from Veterans Affairs. Either there are a lot of wealthy cleaners in the country or the veterans are not being told the truth. I think that there is a good deal more that is being cut than just the heavy house cleaning which the government says is being cut.
The freedom and dignity of veterans to be able to remain in their own homes as long as possible is a right and not a privilege depending on the size of the deficit in this country.
Veterans have fought for their country. They have paid enough. This is the time to honour veterans, not to short change them as this ungrateful government is doing.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Open House Canada was to fund reciprocal group exchange projects for young people across the country and thus increase the awareness of young Canadians in the Abitibi area of their national identity and their desire for unity.
One of this program's priorities was to organize exchanges with rural or isolated communities in Canada, and there was also a special focus on the disabled and the economically disadvantaged.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has dropped this program for direct exchanges between schools effective April 1, 1990, and Le Tremplin secondary school in Malartic is one of the victims.
Mr. Speaker, Canada's isolated areas deserve to see this program maintained. It is a sad commentary that this country's isolated areas have once again been hit by cutbacks.

Mr. Speaker, this past weekend the people of Saskatchewan rallied to support the fourteenth annual Kinsmen Foundation Telemiracle. The telethon raises money to help those in Saskatchewan with physical, mental and emotional disabilities.
This year's effort successfully raised $1.8 million, which is down just slightly from last year. However, given the slow prairie economy it is obvious that we cannot judge the size of the peoples' hearts by the size of their wallets. Under the present economic conditions the level of support for Telemiracle is a tribute to all Saskatchewan people.
I am told that the Kinsmen Telemiracle continues to lead the world in contributions for charity on a per capita basis.
It is apparent that Saskatchewan remains a place where people really do care about their neighbours and their communities. I know that the money raised will be put to good use and that next year's Telemiracle will be bigger than ever.
Congratulations, Kinsmen.

Mr. Speaker, Associate Chief Justice Jerome of the Federal Court, Trial Division, ruled yesterday that the initial humanitarian and compassionate hearing for persons in Canada's 100,000 refugee backlog is illegal and wrongful because the minister's restrictive guidelines contradict Section 114(2) of the Immigration Act.
This means that claimants ought to be admitted on any kind of humanitarian and compassionate grounds.
In view of the huge and growing $200 million mess caused by the government's unconscionable delays and mismanagement of the refugee claims, I call on the Minister of Employment and Immigration immediately
March 6, 1990

to direct immigration staff to use the broad guidelines for long-term de facto residents in Canada as the only basis for all humanitarian and compassionate review of backlog cases.

Mr. Speaker, after 17 days of stubborn resistance the Hagersville tire fire is finally out.
Day after day I watched heavy equipment operators and volunteer fire-fighters work long hours in smoke, heat and mud. They left their jobs and their farms to fight the fire. Evacuees were taken in by friends and family.
The people of Haldimand-Norfolk have really shown us the meaning of community.
We have learned a lot about environmental disasters in the past three weeks. There is still a lot to be learned with the clean up and determining what environmental damage still may exist.
What is abundantly clear is the competent way in which the volunteer fire-fighters did their jobs and conquered the blaze. On behalf of the residents of Haldimand-Norfolk and members of the House I extend our gratitude and thanks for a job well done.
In recognition of the dedicated teamwork that is characteristic of volunteer fire-fighters across Canada, I would ask members of the House to support my motion to increase the present $500 tax exemption on honorariums these fire-fighters receive when it comes before the House. It is the least Canada can do to recognize the great contribution these volunteers make to our country.

Mr. Speaker, one of Canada's efforts to go global has met with success in Japan recently with the sale of 250 tonnes of beef to that country. There is also the potential for further sales in this major growth market outside North America.
The Canadian Beef Export Federation has opened an office in Tokyo. This is seen as a positive step by Japanese companies, one which will facilitate information dispersal and promote new ideas.
Agricultural producers must continue to look to the Pacific Rim countries as potential future markets and initiate the promotion of our many agricultural resources.

Mr. Speaker, where is this government's sense of justice and reality in the priorities it chose for spending cuts?
Democracy is threatened by the slashing of $23 million in Secretary of State funding for native people, ethnic minorities and women's programs. These cuts will eliminate community services, publications and advocacy groups that are essential for powerless groups struggling to achieve equality.
At the same time as $23 million is being cut from these citizen organizations over $23 million will be spent to cover program expenditures of the decadent, unelected, patronage ridden Senate of Canada.
Women's programs which operate on a shoe string were cut by $1.6 million, while $1.6 million will be spent just to renovate committee rooms of the Senate. Women's centres that provide sanctuary, support and services for abused women, visible minority and immigrant women, poor women and those who are working long hours for equality will be forced to close, while $1.6 million desperately needed by these women will be spent to replace red carpets and gold trimming for an outdated, redundant Senate.
I call on this uncaring government to celebrate International Women's Week by changing its priorities and reinstating funding for women's programs and women's centres across Canada.
Let's abolish the Senate in favour of citizen democracy.

Mr. Speaker, last week the Canadian Coast Guard held a

public meeting with residents of Grand Manan Island to discuss plans to destaff the lighthouse on Gannet Rock.
This light located in the middle of the Bay of Fundy is an important navigational device for the hundreds of ships travelling to and from the Port of Saint John. The Irving Oil Company alone ships over 50 million barrels of crude oil through the shipping channels for processing at the refinery.
Fishing and tourism are the pillars of the economy for the residents of Grand Manan. An accident in the Bay of Fundy could cause an environmental disaster in the region and effectively wipe out a way of life that dates back over 100 years.
I urge the Minister of Transport to listen to the concerns raised by the people of Grand Manan and ensure the points they have brought forward will be taken into consideration prior to any final decision on the future of the lighthouse on Gannet Rock.

Mr. Speaker, Canada's crisis in research, science and technology has been further aggravated by the government's decision to cut science and technology spending by $39 million and to reduce transfers to the provinces for education.
The national consortium of scientific and educational societies representing over 500,000 researchers and students is on Parliament Hill this week to tell us that the Prime Minister's rhetoric about doubling our R and D effort is simply not enough.
If Canada is to meet the challenges of a changing world, we must act now.
I urge all members to meet with the consortium and hear its recommendations.
(1)	that there be no further reduction in transfers for post-secondary education;
(2)	that the matching grants policy be incorporated into the base budgets of the granting councils and that these budgets be doubled;
(3)	that R and D performance by the federal government be increased, not diminished; and
(4)	that financial barriers to higher education in Canada be eliminated.

Unless the government acts immediately, Canada will be left behind on the international scene.

Mr. Speaker, last night the finance critic of the Official Opposition, with one wave of his verbal wand, branded several members of the Tory back benches as being among those who opposed the GST.
Today, Mr. Speaker, I stand before you to say that I, the member for Selkirk, support the goods and services tax and, more important, the policies of the government and my colleague, the hon. Minister of Finance.
I say this as a member of the unduly generalized Tory back benches.
The goods and services tax has several advantages which the manufacturers' sales tax does not possess. One of the greatest strengths, of course, is the fact that it will benefit this country and not its foreign competitors. For this reason and many more I support the GST.
I believe the time has come for the Liberal Party to start presenting its own alternatives to the manufacturers' sales tax and stop grandstanding on an empty platform.

Mr. Speaker, this Tory government has stifled debate in the House of Commons on the goods and services tax. It has ignored hundreds of thousands of people who have signed petitions against the GST. It has paid no attention to the thousands of Canadians who have protested the proposed tax through letters and rallies even in the riding of the hon. member who just spoke. The Conservative government does not care what Canadians think about the GST. It just spends money to advertise a tax that has not yet gone through Parliament.
March 6, 1990

The Liberal Party of Canada will continue its battle against this regressive tax. Unlike the Tories, we care about what Canadians think. We want to know how many Canadians oppose the GST.
The Liberal Party is sponsoring a national week of protest against the GST from March 12 to March 16. During this week Canadians from across the country can call 1-900-720-6052 to register their opposition to the tax.
What was the number, Joe?

If Canadians dial 1-900-720-6052 between March 12 and March 16, they will be sending the Prime Minister a clear message that this tax is unacceptable. Together we must make this government listen to the voice of Canadians.
Call 1-900-720-6052.

Mr. Speaker, the people of Canada were able to view clear and distinct choices of the fiscal and taxation plan for Canada as enunciated by the three parties during and after last night's televised debate.
The Conservative plan was well presented and thought out, showing that through a combination of spending restraint, personal income tax reform, corporate tax reform and sales tax reform, combined with increased economic activity in both our domestic markets and offshore markets, Canada would resolve its economic difficulties.
The Liberal plan calls for another study of taxation in Canada. All the previous studies done by the Liberal Party while it was in office would again be ignored and we would embark on a very expensive, probably useless new study.
We would include in this a review of not only taxes under federal jurisdiction but also those under provincial and municipal jurisdiction. As is Liberal policy, the result would be a massive intrusion into the affairs of others by an even bigger central government.
Then there is the NDP. It wants to continue its policy of increasing personal income taxes. Its aim is to kill the goose so that Canada can become a Third World country.
I am happy to say that I support the first plan. Cany on, Mr. Wilson.

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that when Canadians start calling the Liberal line on the GST they should be asking what position of the Liberal Party is that particular person supporting.
This morning in the House the Leader of the Opposition would not say whether or not he would scrap the tax if his party won the next election in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, you could choose a Liberal for almost any position. If you want to scrap the tax, there is the leadership candidate from Hamilton saying yes she would scrap the tax. We also have the finance critic for that party saying they would scrap the tax.
On the other hand, Jean Chretien, the guy who might win the leadership of that party, is saying: "I don't know what I would do if I became prime minister. I may indeed keep that tax".
We also have a Liberal Party document of a few years ago which states that they believe in a value added tax.
Then we have that great leadership candidate from York Weston who is endorsing a flat tax, as is his colleague for Broadview-Greenwood who stole the idea from Peter Pocklington of the Tories in Alberta.
Canadians are asking: Where does the Liberal party stand? Which one are we to believe? What will they do?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship); Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, freedom and democracy are triumphing throughout the world. Across eastern Europe and most recently in Nicaragua people have voted against communist rule and in favour of democratic freedom.
Nowhere is the spark for freedom burning brighter than in the Baltic States. I was honoured to visit Lithuania as a guest of the Canadian Lithuanian Community and the Lithuanian freedom movement, Sajudis,

Oral Questions
to observe their historic elections. The results of those elections sent a clear and unequivocal message of change.
I join with all Canadians in congratulating the people of Lithuania for the elections and for their 50 years of struggle for freedom. The struggle may not yet be over, but the light of freedom is in sight.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. The Deputy Prime Minister will know that this year Environment Canada says there is a strong possibility of drought in the prairie provinces.
1988 was so dry that proper moisture levels have not returned to the soil. A dry fall in 1989 and a lack of snowfall this winter may mean that the soil will still be unable to recharge its moisture content.
Yet, despite this imminent possibility, the government has cut funding for the Canadian Crop Drought Assistance Program from $788 million down to only $21.3 million, a drop of more than 90 per cent.
Why has this fund been cut more than 90 per cent when there is a real possibility that 1990 will be another year of serious drought for our western farmers?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I genuinely appreciate-and I am sure all Canadians will appreciate it-the hon. member's interest in this very important issue. I hope, when the appropriate time comes to act on behalf of the agricultural industry and the prairie regions, that I will have the full support of the hon. member.
As he knows, we have responded in a very major fashion to the difficulties in the agricultural sector all across the country, but more particularly as it relates to western Canada. There has been a record pay-out in drought assistance of some $850 million. Improvements
were made to the crop insurance program. There were enhancements for multi-year drought situations.
We are now in the process of mailing cheques out to the three prairie provinces on the basis of the multi-year disaster benefit program. Alberta and Manitoba have received. The figures for Saskatchewan are not in. As soon as they are in there could be payments going out on supplementary drought up to $80 million.
I should advise the hon. member as well that we are looking at what further assistance might be required.
Also, we are looking at what assistance might be required in terms of providing money, cash flow, to ensure that the crop can be put in as well as the long-term interim support programs.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue is not whether he and the government will have the support of the Official Opposition on this matter, but whether he will have the support of the Minister of Finance. That is the big question.
I have another question for the Deputy Prime Minister.
Last night the premier of Saskatchewan spoke on television and indicated that he had spoken with the Deputy Prime Minister and that the Deputy Prime Minister had agreed, and I quote, "to work out the farm financial crisis".
The Deputy Prime Minister knows that the farm financial crisis affects farmers in many provinces, not just Saskatchewan.
Can the Deputy Prime Minister assure this House and the farmers of Canada today that any financial assistance program for farmers will be available in all the provinces and not simply be confined to one province?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have indicated to the House before, we have put together a federal-provincial review committee to assess the impact of the shortfall and to assess the application of the existing programs, that is the multi-year disaster benefit program which was an enhancement to the crop insurance program incorporated last year.
We also have improvements to the crop insurance program currently before the House which will provide
March 6, 1990

more long-term enhancement for crop disasters arising from drought and other weather conditions.
I can assure the hon. member that as soon as the reports come in from the federal-provincial monitoring committee which affects the industry right across the country we will assess it, look at options and come up with an appropriate program that will be cost shared as has been indicated by the respective Ministers of Agriculture of the provinces.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope western farmers and other farmers across Canada will not have to wait as long for any special program as the fishermen of Atlantic Canada have been waiting. They have hurt a lot and they have got nothing so far.

Mr. Speaker, the Premier of Saskatchewan also said that, together with the Deputy Prime Minister, he would be meeting representatives of our major financial institutions, to determine ways of helping farmers who are having trouble restructuring their debts.
My question for the Deputy Prime Minister is this: Can he guarantee that the government will make the banks and various loan institutions help our farmers restructure their debts? Can he also guarantee before this House that he will take action before all family farms in this country have disappeared? Could he answer this question right away?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is quite true that I have met with the premier of Saskatchewan. It is recognized that the problem in Saskatchewan is very critical because of the drought and because of its particular type of agriculture, which is basically grain and oilseeds.
The problem is threefold. First, there is the issue of the current shortage of cash to get the crop in. Second, there is the long-term debt situation. Third, it relates to the long-term income support program which is part and parcel of the agricultural review.
As the hon. member should know, the grain stabilization programs and the safety nets that have been in place
Oral Questions
have been put through the supreme test. We are in the process of re-evaluating and re-examining in an attempt to come up with better safety nets. That process is ongoing.
Whatever we do in the course of providing long-term income support, we hope that it can lead to a longer term support system.
In so far as his reference to the banks is concerned, yes, we do meet on a regular basis. Inasmuch as we have met on previous occasions with the banks and other lending institutions, we will be undertaking the same thing to ensure that there is that kind of compassion to which the hon. member refers.
I should also point out that the farm debt review board was an initiative of this government and that process has gone a long way to alleviating some of the difficulties and the hardships as they relate to farmers who are found to be in serious difficulty in defraying their payments and dealing with their long-term debt program. We intend to continue to work in that regard as well.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the two ministers responsible for immigration, I direct my question to the Deputy Prime Minister.
Yesterday, in a landmark ruling, the Federal Court ruled that the government's system to process the over 125,000 refugee claimants in the refugee backlog is illegal. This ruling serves to confirm the concerns that we on this side of the House have been expressing and raising with the government for months on end.
In light of this fatal blow from the Federal Court, will the government do the right and appropriate thing and abandon its current refugee backlog clearance system and replace it immediately with a fair, more efficient, more humane administrative review, something that the Official Opposition had asked this government for over one year ago?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Danis (Minister of State (Youth) and Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Employment and Immigration has not yet had an opportunity to study the reasons for the court's decision, as the court has yet to release those reasons. It would therefore be prema-

March 6, 1990
Oral Questions
ture to comment upon the possible impact of the decision.
However, the Minister of Employment and Immigration and her officials have had an opportunity to review Justice Jerome's oral reasons, and appropriate decisions will be made quickly as to how the government will react.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I wish to also congratulate the minister who has been elevated to cabinet with new responsibilities. Not to undermine his appointment, the refugee claimants, the system and Canadians deserve a better answer.
I would like to put my question again to the Deputy Prime Minister. The government cannot run or hide from the reality that the backlog system has been universally condemned, whether by the NGOs, the parliamentary committee or the legal entities of our country.
Given that only 6 per cent of all claimants have been processed, that it will take six years to clear the backlog at the present rate at a $200 million expense and at an increased human expense in terms of human misery, why is the government stubbornly refusing in the face of this mounting opposition simply to repeal and fix not only a broken system, but a system that has now been rendered illegal by our courts?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Danis (Minister of State (Youth) and Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the hon. member that each person in the backlog has made a claim to be a convention refugee and therefore is entitled to a decision on the merits of that claim. The primary question, therefore, continues to be one of refugee determination.
This government is aware of the concerns of backlog claimants and of the interest of Canadians in seeing this issue resolved. We will respond to Justice Jerome's decision as quickly as possible but cannot at this time engage in speculation which can only add to the uncertainty experienced by backlog claimants.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
In the recent budget the Minister of Finance and this government cut $3 billion from programs which aid battered women, the regions, support post-secondary education and provide minimal assistance to the poor, as well as other programs that address those areas in our society.
At the same time tax breaks for large corporations were allowed, and I cite some examples. Brascan earned some $262 million last year and paid not one cent. Edper Enterprises made $52 million and paid not one cent. Fletcher Challenge made $24 million and paid not one cent.
Is it not now time to introduce a minimum corporate tax so that everyone pays their fair share?

Mr. Speaker, as a result of a number of decisions that this government has taken both in corporate income tax reform in 1987-88, as well as a number of other times during the course of the past five years, we have removed many, many tax loopholes that large corporations have been using. There are reasons individual corporations that are profitable are not paying taxes.
If she wants to identify a specific tax provision that she wants to see removed that allows for these corporations not to pay tax, one of them being the fact that they have losses in previous years and carry forward those losses to apply against current year profits and apply their taxes on that, then let us listen to and hear what she has to say.
I hear again that she is calling for a corporate minimum tax of 20 per cent. Small businesses pay a corporate tax of 12 per cent. How is she going to deal with the thousands and thousands of small businesses which are only paying 12 per cent tax?

My supplementary is directed to the Minister of Finance. In his budget, the Minister cut transfer payments for health and postsecondary education by about one billion dollars this year and 1.5 billion for next year.
March 6, 1990

Meanwhile, deductions for business meals and entertainment have been maintained. These deductions represent a total of nearly one billion dollars annually.
Will the Minister of Finance finally decide to abolish these deductions which are unacceptable and make the government lose such vast amounts of money?

Mr. Speaker, these deductions are important to businesses competing with the United States that have that precise same tax deduction. We need a tax system in Canada that is competitive with the United States. This is very important to the creation of jobs in Canada.
If we are to have a corporate tax system that is not competitive with the United States, that has higher tax rates than the United States, then a very simple result will happen.
Companies are going to settle in the United States. They will create new investment in the United States and with that jobs will be created in the United States and not in Canada.
If the New Democratic Party policy is to move jobs from Canada to the United States, then that is exactly what will happen with the policies that she is proposing.

Mr. Speaker, the biggest policy which has moved jobs from Canada to the United States is the trade deal and the minister knows that. I also remind the minister that the United States has a minimum corporate tax.
In 1987, when the Minister of Finance introduced the budget he said and I quote:
Our fundamental strategy in reviewing the corporate income tax is
to ensure that profitable corporations pay their fair share. We must
further reduce the source of the problem by cutting back special
corporate tax write-offs.
In spite of that promise, corporate profits that escape tax have grown from $15 billion to $27 billion since he took that job. How does the minister justify these tax cuts to large corporations when he is asking every Canadian to pay an extra 7 per cent through the goods and services tax?
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has raised four specific points in that question and I want to address each one of them.
First, in the last couple of years we have had very high levels of investment in this country directly related to companies getting ready for the free trade agreement, and that has created jobs here in Canada. It has created a more competitive Canadian economy precisely as a result of the free trade agreement.
The second point that my hon. colleague makes is that there is a corporate minimum tax in the United States. She is correct. There is also a much higher tax rate on small businesses in the United States. Is she proposing that we increase the tax rate on small business so we can have a corporate minimum tax here? I do not think so but that is the result of the question that she has asked.
The third point I make is that corporations today are paying more tax, including corporations that were not paying any tax before. Her colleagues have asked in the past how a bank teller could pay more tax than the bank itself. As a result of corporate income tax reform in 1988, banks today are now paying hundreds of millions of dollars of corporate tax, directly as a result of corporate tax reform.
The final point that I would make with my colleague in response to her question is that corporate profits are down this year. That is one reason why corporate taxes are down. If she looks at the effective corporate tax rate this year compared with 1987 she will see that the effective corporate tax rate is up this year compared to three years ago.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture, the Deputy Prime Minister. Last November I asked the minister what action he was prepared to take in light of the demand by the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool and other groups like the Ontario Com Producers to assist in the farm financial crisis facing farmers right across the country. Since November the situation has worsened: moisture levels are low, world grain prices are low, farm debt is worse and interest rates have risen.

March 6, 1990
Oral Questions
Why do the Deputy Prime Minister and the government refuse to act in light of this tragedy facing Canadian farmers?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the federal government is not refusing to act. It is very active in assessing the magnitude of the difficulties and trying to bring about and look at a number of options.
We are still waiting for the preliminary crop data from the province of Saskatchewan so we can send out the supplementary drought benefit payments which are due to them as a result of the enhanced crop insurance program that we put in place last year. We must have that information before we can accurately define the problem. When we accurately define the problem we will accurately provide a solution.

Mr. Speaker, in 1986 the Prime Minister provided $1 billion when the Premier of Saskatchewan was facing a political disaster in the middle of an election campaign.
Now, tens of thousands of farmers face the loss of the land, including the premier himself. With seeding only two months away, can the minister say when he is going to act? Is he going to respond to the demand the premier made last night that at least $500 million be provided for spring seeding, which is only a couple of months away, so that these farmers can get ready for the crop year? Will he provide the equivalent proportionate amount of money to other farmers across the country? Will the Deputy Prime Minister respond?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I indicated to the hon. member earlier, we are assessing the magnitude of the difficulty and are trying to devise some options that will respond to that difficulty.
As I indicated, we are eager to send out supplementary drought cheques. The cheques have gone out to the province of Manitoba and the province of Alberta under the multi-year disaster program. Saskatchewan could be receiving up to $80 million under that particular program depending upon the figures, when they come in.
We are also looking at what might be necessary in terms of short term cash flow necessity, as well as the longer term income support which hopefully can be tied into a long term safety net proposal that is currently being discussed by a special committee that was set up. We are not stepping away from the problem; we have not in the past, we are not today and we won't in the future.
* * #

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. He has just heard his colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, commit to providing major assistance to farmers across Canada as they face drought conditions, financial debt problems and increasing international competition.
I have a very simple question for the Minister of Finance. Where is the money going to come from? The Minister of Finance has cut the drought assistance estimates by $736 million. He has cut the reserve fund by 47 per cent. He has committed to the financial markets to hold the deficit line at $28.5 billion to meet his interest rate projections. There is no flexibility, no reserve and no contingency.
Will the Minister of Finance guarantee today that he will live up to the financial commitment?

Mr. Speaker, what I will commit to today is that I will not go through with the spending record of the former Liberal governments: 1969 to 1970, 1970 to 1974, 17.9 per cent annual increase; 1979-80 to 1984-85, 14 per cent.
We have held our spending at 3.6 per cent. We are committed to holding it this year to a 3 per cent increase.
Answer the question, Mike.

The answer to the question is that we have taken the prudent action of having reserves that are in our spending program this year so we can respond to contingencies like my colleagues talks about in the agricultural sector-
When?

-like colleagues opposite have asked on the fisheries issues. We have moneys-
March 6, 1990
We haven't seen it. We have gone bankrupt.
Well now the hon. member's mouth is moving faster than her brain.
Do something. People are going down.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance is simply blowing in the wind. He knows that his government has made commitments to bail out fishermen. He is now saying they have money in the reserve fund for the farmers, but he has cut the reserve fund by 47 per cent.
There is no money there to meet these commitments. We want to know when this government is going to speak straight with the Canadian farmers and when it is going to answer the premier of Saskatchewan who said the federal government has now declared war on the prairie provinces? When is this government going to stop declaring war and start helping the fundamental farm and fish sectors of this economy?

Mr. Speaker, I think we have demonstrated clearly in the past that when there is a problem we will address it. We have indicated clearly that there are amounts of money in the reserves. When the consultation process described by the Minister of Agriculture has been completed, then we will be in a position to announce that.
In the case of fisheries, when consultations are completed on the question of fisheries, then we will be able to announce the additional-
When? You said that a year ago.
Now the hon. member from Yarmouth keeps yelling over there, and she should realize that we have already-
You don't know. You don't see the people.
Mr. Speaker, maybe you should advise the hon. member that it is hard to hear when her mouth is going all the time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for Mackenzie.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. I note in his responses on the agricultural question that both he and the Minister of Finance seem to think what they have is a problem with an old drought.
I would like to switch their attention to a more current problem, the problem of not being able to be competitive with the United States because our assistance programs do not match theirs, something the Minister of Finance alluded to, and the problem of the continuing escalation of the war between the Americans and the Europeans to reduce world grain prices.
Canada had an almost statistically average crop last year and yet incomes are falling to the point where there is less than zero realized net income expected in the province of Saskatchewan this year. Where is the aid that the Deputy Prime Minister has been promising would come in recompense against those grain wars? We have six weeks until seeding starts and banks are refusing to give money to farmers until they know where they stand. When will he announce, who will get it and how much will it be?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's question and the sincerity with which he asks it. I can respond in an equally sincere manner.
The fact of the matter is that we have put together a federal-provincial committee to assess the situation and to look at the application of existing programs. Quite frankly, unbeknown to most farmers, they are going to be receiving supplementary drought assistance payments as a result of the multi-year crop disaster enhancement that was put in place.
We are looking to see how that will fill that particular void. We are looking at ways and means of coming up with some cash flow to help farmers put their crops in. We are looking at the long term income system and hopefully that can be tied to improvements in the safety net.
This government has responded to the international price wars in the past. It is prepared to do so again. But I remind the hon. member that the level of enhancement has reduced quite substantially. In 1986 and 1987, the EEP was subsidizing grain and oilseeds to the tune of

March 6, 1990
Oral Questions
about $200 per tonne, today it is about $80 per tonne. The United States is subsidizing under the EEP about $20 per tonne. In the meantime grain prices have increased between 1986 and 1989 by roughly 50 per cent.
All of those things have to be taken into consideration and I am sure my hon. friend will realize that you cannot merely pull a figure out of the sky. We are assessing the magnitude of the problem, we are assessing it accurately and we are going to respond in an accurate and full manner.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that the hon. minister is trying to do something. He said so numerous times in this House and thousands of other farmers believe him as well. But the banks will not lend money on that. When is he going to put some dollars up so that we can decide whether we are going to have farmers putting in crops or farmers leaving the farms. That is what it has come to as far as most of the banks are concerned right now.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can advise the hon. member that we have been working on this matter since the first of the year. The initial reports are coming in but I remind him again that at the present time we are waiting for crop insurance data from the province of Saskatchewan to complete the payments under the multi-year disaster program. This is the kind of information that we need. We are now in the process of looking at what the initial prices will be and I am sure my hon. friend will recognize that all of those things have to be taken into consideration before a full solution can be provided.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Transport. The Banff Chamber of Commerce reports that business in its area appears to have slowed down this winter, in part due to the VIA Rail cuts. VIA has received many proposals for the privatization of a system to supply rail services between Calgary and Vancouver.
When can the people of this area expect the resumption of a continuous rail service, a service which is crucial to their livelihood and which was promised to them by the previous minister?
Mr. Speaker-
Hear, hear!

I am a little nervous when the opposition claps too.
I wish to advise the member that proposals for privatization have been received. The bids closed on January 15.1 am advised that VIA is examining the bids, and they expect to be in a position to make a recommendation to the government by the end of March.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Immigration my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister.
Yesterday, the Federal Court quashed Conservative legislation that was supposed to deal with the backlog of applications for refugee status.
The minister is aware that the refugee backlog is estimated at more than 100,000, and that many claimants have been waiting for a decision for three years. The saddest cases are those where parents have been separated from their children for several years, pending a decision allowing them to enter Canada.
Mr. Speaker, is the government at least prepared to allow these children to be reunited with their parents who have sought refuge in Canada, until a decison has been handed down in their case?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Danis (Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport); Minister of State (Youth); Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are of course aware of the judgment that was handed down yesterday by the former Speaker of the House of Commons, Mr. Justice Jerome. We are now looking at the situation and considering the judgment, and we will give our response as soon as possible.
March 6, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I will direct my supplementary question to the chairman of the Standing Committee on Immigration.
It is wrong to keep human beings waiting so long without a decision, and it is even worse to keep them separated from their young children. This problem requires a humanitarian approach, not a legalistic one.
The Standing Committee on Immigration conducted a long study on this matter and put out an important report in December in which it made serious recommendations to the government to improve the refugee situation.
Will the chairman of the committee call a meeting of the committee as soon as possible, call the minister before the committee and have her explain to the committee what she is going to do about this decision of the Federal Court and impress upon her the recommendations of the standing committee to speed up this process?

Mr. Speaker, tomorrow the steering committee of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration will meet in order to study the judgment handed down yesterday by Mr. Justice Jerome, as well as other business to be undertaken by the Standing Committee including the Estimates which are also on the agenda for tomorrow. Of course, tomorrow, we will start analysing the report we tabled in the House on the refugee backlog which is directly related to the judgment.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Veterans Affairs.
Why did he say yesterday that there were no cuts in veterans' benefits when reduction in the veterans' inde-
Oral Questions
pendence program in the words of the recent budget at page 84 "will save an estimated $18 million"? Why?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerald S. Merrithew (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yesterday they were talking about budget cuts. I mention again that there were no cuts in the actual dollars of expenditures in the department, and in fact with the veterans' independence program, there are major increases in that spending.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is directed to the same minister, who said: "I assure the hon. member that there have been no cuts made at all".
The government's own documents state that the veterans receiving assistance under the veterans independence program, which is designed to care for them at home, will no longer be reimbursed for heavy housekeeping services to the tune of $18 million.
The average age of Canada's veterans is 70 and this is an essential service to them. This $18 million cut is counter to the aim of this program. I would like to ask the Minister of Veterans Affairs why he has allowed this to happen.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerald S. Merrithew (Minister of Veterans Affairs):

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity, unexpected though it is at this very moment, to participate in the budget debate. I am very proud to have the opportunity to address this House on what I consider to be an outstanding 1990 budget.
Following a steady course since 1984, the Minister of Finance has again constructed a budget for the coming fiscal year which directs Canada toward financial integrity and economic responsibility. In so doing, the government will be compelled to introduce some difficult and initially unpopular expense control measures, but for the first time in more than two decades we have a federal budget with no new taxes.
Thus, we see a budget plan that responds to the demands and the needs which have been expressed by Canadians. For many months now, the message from all parts of the country has been clear; continue the attack on the debt and the deficit, but intensify the strategy to cut spending and do not increase the tax burden at all. This budget reflects that strategy in very strong and sound ways.
In actual fact, however, if there is any one major criticism which I have heard about this budget, it is that the budget does not go far enough. The national will for financial discipline is very strong indeed and the average citizen fully supports a government mandate to put our financial house in order. What that average citizen demands, though, is evidence and commitment that the
measures which have been taken will truly be applied to solve Canada's financial problems, and not merely used to support or expand government spending programs. This budget provides such assurances in a very clear manner.
First of all, it confirms the accuracy and integrity of the current year's Estimates, which will result in a deficit of $30.5 billion as predicted one year ago. This is a remarkable accomplishment in its own right, because the past year has been fraught with unexpected economic adversities such as persistent inflation and high short-term interest rates. Fortunately, the economy has remained relatively strong, employment has remained at high levels and government revenues have increased as a result. Longer term interest rates have declined somewhat to help moderate government debt service expense. The net result is that the 1989 deficit forecast is right on the money, which is a continuing basis for confidence in the 1990 Estimates and in the five-year forward projections which accompany it.
The budget aims for a steadily falling deficit over the next five years and onward to balanced budgets and eventually, I hope, to surpluses after that. The deficit will be $28.5 billion in the new fiscal year and $26.8 billion in the 1992 budget. It is predicted that we shall be able to start redeeming bonds and paying down some of our national debt in the 1994 period.
Just imagine for a moment-that will prove the first time in 20 years Canada has actually lived within its means for a full fiscal year. What stronger or clearer commitment could any government make in response to its financial mandate.
The deficit targets for the next two years deserve special mention because they reflect significant provisions of $2 billion in extraordinary expense in each of those periods to pay major start-up costs of the goods and services tax program as it replaces the federal sales tax system commencing on January 1, 1991.
These costs will really be significant benefits to many Canadians-advance rebates of almost $1 billion as promised to low-income families before the GST even commences in December of this year, and about $3 billion to Canadian businesses for GST rebates on existing FST-included inventories and for one-time
March 6, 1990

payment of transitional expense up to $1,000 per business.
Here is hard evidence of the practical benefits which the goods and services tax program will bring to low-income Canadians and to many small and large Canadian companies. We have clearly budgeted $4 million, with cheques to be issued over the next 24 months. Here is hard evidence also of the deficit reduction progress really to be found in this budget.
Without these extraordinary one-time expenses, the next two years would be $2 billion lower in each case. Once those expenditures are out of the way, the subsequent diminishing deficit projections between 1992 and 1994 become all the more credible at $21 billion, $14 billion, and $10 billion respectively. Truly we can now see light at the end of Canada's financial tunnel.
That this 1990 budget marks a crossroads in Canada's financial affairs has never been in doubt, and the directions to be taken have been hotly debated in every comer of the country. The options have been advanced in a variety of policy formats: new taxes, moderate spending, drastic expense cuts, lower interest rates, higher inflation, a lower dollar, increased exports and so on. But in my view, the proper course has been selected.
With our national debt at $350 billion and growing at the rate of almost 10 per cent per year-and it could touch as high as $.5 trillion before we turn it around- this government is taking the tough tack through perilous waters, where the reefs have names like "recession" and "inflation", but where also lies the charted course toward calmer financial seas and toward fairer winds for future economic growth.
The restraint measures of this budget should help to contain inflation, which in turn should help to moderate interest rates, which then in turn should also stimulate renewed economic growth within our stable capacity to manage it.
I feel confident that this approach is the right one, that recession can be avoided and that stability and new progress will be achieved. This budget is not only a tough and a responsible one, it is also a fair and a sensitive one. Again, to ensure emphasis, it bears no new taxes. But even more important, there are several critical exemptions for people from the expense-control plans, namely, elderly benefits, family allowances, veterans pensions, and unemployment insurance payments. These constitute a continuing shift of the budget and taxation burden off the shoulders of low-income Canadians and are
The Budget
consistent with such measures introduced in previous budgets of the Minister of Finance and in tax reform bills.
Slowly but surely taxation relief and social security are being put in fair balance in Canada for those most in need of them.
Perhaps the most telling and yet sensitive policy initiatives for expense control in this budget are to be found in restraints applied to provincial transfer payments. As was expressed so well in a Montreal Gazette editorial last week, the funds for all levels of government come from the same ultimate taxpayer, so it is nonsensical to expect federal transfers to provinces to remain untouched when they constitute such a major item of federal spending.
To their credit, many provinces have been balancing their budgets, but this becomes a sort of phantom accounting when large portions of their revenue come from a federal budget which is on the edge of insolvency. Clearly, the provinces' transfers are part of the national financial problem, and so they must realistically be part of the solution. As a result, Established Programs Financing has been frozen per capita at 1989 budget levels and Canada Assistance Plan transfers will be limited to a growth of 5 per cent annually in Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia.
What is most significant in terms of this budget's fairness and sensitivity is the fact that all other provinces which qualify for equalization payments will be exempted from the CAP limits, as will the equalization program itself be exempted from the expense control plan. Equalization payments will continue to flow to the provinces in the same proportions as they have traditionally.
These exemptions are an innovative recognition that regional economic disparities and imbalances do exist in Canada and that reciprocating advantages must be provided to fairly balance the application of economic policies. This is not possible with some options such as interest rates where selective application would be non-viable but the unbalanced approach to restraint measures as used in this budget do go far to achieving a fair balance of economic policy right across Canada. For example, total federal transfer payments to Atlantic Canada will grow at the rate of 4 per cent in the coming year while they will also be held to a rate of only 2.3 per cent in Ontario. That does seem fair, given the compara-

The Budget
tive levels of economic activity between Atlantic Canada and Ontario.
In fact, in my own province of New Brunswick, the Liberal government of Premier McKenna has publicly expressed acceptance of, if not support for, this 1990 federal budget. Although the new restraint measures do have significant impact on New Brunswick to the tune of $25 million in 1990 and almost twice as much in 1991, nevertheless these reductions amount to less than 1 per cent of total provincial revenues.
By contrast, the aggregate of all federal transfers to New Brunswick year after year, account for more than 40 per cent of all New Brunswick's budget revenues. As in New Brunswick, so is the case with most other provinces. No group should be more vitally concerned about supporting the financial health of the federal government than the finance ministers of those provinces and their premiers.
The opposition financial critic has been quick to claim that restraints on provincial transfers will lead to higher taxation by the provinces. His case is weak in the extreme. For example, in New Brunswick the provincial government indicates that it should be able to balance its own 1990 budget and acknowledges that program spending restraint to follow the federal example may be the most reasonable course. Perhaps federal Liberals should consult with their provincial colleagues to learn and understand that small "c" conservative financial responsibility is conventional wisdom these days in Canada and that big "C" Conservative financial policies are receiving strong public support.
One of the best cases to be made in this regard is the disciplined containment of federal program spending over the past five years at 3.6 per cent annually, less than the rate of inflation. By comparison, the provincial average over that same period has been almost twice as high at 6.4 per cent with some provinces, notably Ontario, increasing their spending at rates well over 9 per cent.
Simply put, the federal example of program spending restraint is the best in the nation and has been posed in this budget as an essential challenge for the provinces to emulate. Far from promoting increased taxes, this budget sets a model for financial discipline. The federal example of 3.7 per cent restrained growth in program spending over the next two years clearly demonstrates to the provinces that more can be done to limit expenditures.
In the same context, the premature conclusions by opposition representatives that a two-year freeze on EPF transfers will directly result in cuts to education and health are invalid. As they well realize, or should know, EPF funds are no longer restricted and the provinces have been using this money in a variety of ways for several years. In effect, EPF is now virtually block funding and does not hobble the financial flexibility of any province to select its own spending priorities. There is simply no valid reason why education or health should become special targets as a result of this budget.
Tb the contrary in fact, the granting councils, the National Sciences and Engineering Research Council, the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council and the Medical Research Council, which provide research support to universities, have been specifically relieved from the 5 per cent CAP applied to other areas of science and technology in this budget.
It is very significant that these granting councils have been specifically relieved of the 5 per cent limitation applied to all other areas of science and technology and that should be recognized by those in the fields of education and health as a very significant and appropriate measure in the budget.
The provinces will bear close to one-third of the $3 billion expenditure savings contained in this budget, which is a moderate share in a major national mission toward financial responsibility, particularly considering the fact that funding to the provinces over the past five years has consistently consumed 23 per cent of all federal program spending in cash terms.
As federal debt has risen to support these and other major costs, the federal budget for debt service has grown to 35.1 cents of every revenue dollar. By comparison, the average provincial debt is serviced by only one-third of that amount or 11.8 cents of every revenue dollar. Even in Atlantic Canada provincial debt service is less than 15 per cent of revenues. So again, simply put, the provinces rightly share the benefits of the federal

purse and they must also rightly share the burden of the debt against it.
For my own province of New Brunswick, it is worth noting some of the key implications of this 1990 federal budget. Total federal transfers will increase to New Brunswick by almost 4.5 per cent in 1990 and will total well over $1.5 billion, more than 40 per cent of the total provincial budget. No direct cuts have been made, except that per capita EPF grants are frozen for the next two years at current levels. This represents less than 1 per cent of New Brunswick budget revenues and is a restraint on future expectations and not on present funding.
Federal transfers will average approximately $2,100 per citizen in New Brunswick during the coming year, the third highest in the nation after Newfoundland and P.E.I. Major federal projects in the province remain uninterrupted, notably the frigate construction program in Saint John and the combat training centre at CFB Gagetown. By contrast some multibillion dollar projects were totally cancelled in other parts of Canada. As announced late last week, the ACOA program, which is so vital to Atlantic Canada, has not been reduced and, in fact, additional new areas of activity such as marketing will be supported and funding limits have been extended to provide for larger projects.
On balance, therefore, and particularly by comparison with larger more affluent provinces, this budget recognizes the special economic circumstances of New Brunswick and the entire Atlantic region.
As most Canadians understand, our country has been living beyond its means for a long, long time. That is what deficit financing means, spending more each year than we are prepared to pay for or can afford. To the credit of this government, in 1984 it recognized the dread disease of deficit and debt in Canada and embarked upon an agenda for economic renewal as a long-term course toward cure and recovery from our nation's financial illness. The facts of their success are revealing, particularly in operating budget terms when you separate debt service from operating revenues.
Mr. Speaker, I am coming quickly to a close. In 1984 we were not even remotely covering program expenditures and we had an operating deficit of $16 billion as
The Budget
part of the total deficit of $38 billion. In the current year now ending, only five years later, we shall have an operating surplus of $9 billion, unfortunately still as part of a continuing total deficit of $30.5 billion.
The striking reality is that we have achieved major progress in bringing program spending under control. In that five-year period an operating deficit of $16 billion has been turned to a surplus of $9 billion, a net gain of $25 billion.
Time obviously does not permit me to address the many other important issues and detailed Estimates contained in this budget. I have described the features which I believe bear special mention.
Over-all, this budget is another major move in a consistent direction toward financial integrity for Canada and it is one which I endorse and support fully.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great intensity to the member's speech. I want to ask him two basic questions. One deals with the issue of confidence that the Canadian public has in the Minister of Finance.
Last year when the minister presented his budget, he said that the interest rate would be 10.5 per cent at this time. It is now closer to 13.5 per cent; an error of 30 per cent. Three years ago the Minister of Finance said that by this current year the deficit would be reduced to about $14 billion. It is closer to $30 billion; an error of 100 per cent. Now the Minister of Finance is giving nice rosy projections as to what is going to happen in 1994 and 1995. Why should the Canadian public believe him when his previous predictions turned out to be totally unreliable? Second, the government keeps saying that there is a need to reduce the deficit, to cut spending. I want to ask the member how, in light of the need for reduced spending, government members can support the bill as they did last week? How can they bring in a mass tax concession in terms of increased RRSP contributions for the wealthy, increasing it by another $400 million for those earning between $50,000 and $86,000, bringing the total tax concessions on RRSP contributions to people earning in excess of $50,000-which is the the same as losing taxes-to $11 billion this year? If there is such a

March 6, 1990
The Budget
shortage of money, why did the government proceed to give more tax concessions to its wealthy friends?
I want those two questions addressed. What confidence does the public have in the Minister of Finance? His predictions in the past have been totally erroneous. Why, if there is a need to reduce the deficit, is the government still giving away tax concessions to its wealthy friends?

Mr. Speaker, the public of Canada does have extreme confidence in the Minister of Finance, and well they should have. The Minister of Finance last year predicted that the deficit in 1989-90 would be $30.5 billion. He has been faced since that time with a number of extraordinary circumstances, such as increasing inflation and increasing interest rates. Yet, he is coming in right on the money at $30.5 billion. His predictions over the history of his tenure have been exceedingly accurate on balance. I believe there is good cause, particularly given the improvements in the operating surplus position as I have described in my remarks, to believe that we will see the deficit predictions that he has made met on the money-$26.8 billion in 1991, $21 billion in 1992, $14 billion in 1993 and $10 billion in 1994.
Just imagine, in 1994 the deficit will be cut by two-thirds from present levels and the government will be in a position to start redeeming its bonds and paying down its debt for the first time in a quarter century. The people of Canada will have immense confidence in this finance minister for decades after that.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member for Fredericton-York-Sun-bury said something that has me somewhat puzzled. In fairness to him, the subject is education. His government, on the one hand, has instructed the Canada Manpower Centres to put emphasis on training in a province like Newfoundland where those who complete the training have no jobs to go to. That is not a euphemism. That is not a catch phrase. It is not a partisan phrase. It is a fact of life. They do their training, they go to the community colleges and take computer training to do all kinds of things and then they turn around and there are no jobs for them to go to. The emphasis on training might be good for Tbronto and
other parts of Canada but it is certainly not good for my constituency in Newfoundland and, I would suggest to the hon. member, maybe for parts of his area.
The other half of this coin is that this training that the Manpower Centres insist on precludes the smaller communities from employing its people on the small infrastructure development projects that certainly were in vogue when I first became a member of Parliament. That employment, in some cases, is the only means of qualifying for UIC. They are the only jobs that they can get, so you get community infrastructure and you get jobs. But that is all gone now because they have to go off and do training and in some cases the people cannot qualify. Communities end up with no infrastructure. So right now there is no aid package for the economic crisis and no jobs for job development programs.
On the other hand, this government says that it is bent on training, but the Minister of Finance, in his budget, has put together what is considered to be, by most people in the business, a loss to the post-secondary education of $9 billion by 1995. I cannot understand this dichotomy. Where are we heading? Are we for training and education or are we not?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as someone once said, if you think education is worthless, try ignorance. The facts are that Newfoundlanders are not ignorant and Newfoundlanders recognize, I am sure, as even the hon. member recognizes behind his rhetoric, that training, innovation and creativity do constitute the solution to some of the structural economic and unemployment circumstances in which we find ourselves, such as the fishery.
If the resource is gone, depleted through a variety of causes, we cannot simply reside there in blissful dependence forever on any government. I do not believe Newfoundlanders want that. I believe Newfoundlanders do want training, they do want to be educated and pointed in new directions. That is what is going to happen.
