subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to participate for the first time as Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in the budget debate. Needless to say, it is with much enthusiasm and confidence in the future that I approach this new mandate which the Right Hon. Prime Minister has given to me. I would like to tell you, Mr. Speaker, and this House that I will fulfil my new responsibilities to the best of my knowledge and with a great deal of energy. I will also continue to discharge the important responsibilities of my position as Minister of State for Agriculture with the same interest and dedication.
The Budget tabled in this House on February 20 by the Hon. Minister of Finance, Mr. Speaker, is quite in keeping with the policy of fiscal responsibility that our government has pursued for the past five years. This Budget brings us closer to our objective of reducing the deficit by 1994 while taking account-and I think this is important-of the immediate needs of people of modest means. This is a big challenge, a difficult challenge, but I believe that we now have all the tools in hand to meet it.
When we came to power in 1984, the economy and public finances were in disastrous shape. I do not need to remind this House of what the size of the deficit, the unemployment rate and inflation were then then, and also the interest rates that had ruined many of our businesses.
Correcting this situation, Mr. Speaker, required more than cosmetic measures and improvised policies. It took a long-term policy, a real action program to put Canada back on the road to economic prosperity. That is what we proposed then. The Minister of Finance, the same one as today, offered Canadians a comprehensive, articulate, multi-year plan that would enable Canadians to prepare the future.
The Budget
This plan, Mr. Speaker, was based on two main thrusts, two priority areas for action: first, restoring the public finances and second, creating a favourable climate for measures to stimulate economic growth.
We therefore took strong measures to reduce the deficit which then was approaching $40 billion, as you will recall. We first attacked public expenditures, especially program spending which at that time was more than government revenues and was growing at a frightening rate of 14 per cent a year. At the time, people would say that the government was borrowing to pay for the groceries.
Over the next five years, this growth rate in program spending was brought down to 3.6 per cent. That was real belt-tightening. It would have been difficult, really difficult, Mr. Speaker, to be credible when we asked Canadians to tighten their belts if the government for its part took the attitude that it could continue to spend more than its income by increasing its spending inconsiderately. We therefore began by tightening our own belt as a government.
We also reduced the size of the Public Service by 12,000 person-years. We have in fact returned to the 1973 level; the size of the Public Service is what it was 17 years ago, with the result that today government spending is less in dollar terms than it was five years ago.
Mr. Speaker, we also transferred to the private sector Crown corporations that no longer met the objectives for which they had been created and that also were running deficits. Today, not only are these companies no longer a burden for the government but they have become prosperous enterprises contributing to Canada's economic growth. It was a step we had to take. We took it and we will continue to do so over the years, Mr. Speaker.
If we had not introduced these measures, the government's Budget would be $22 billion more than it is today. However, to turn around the economy, we not only had to put our financial house in order, we also had to adopt measures that would allow the private sector to develop its potential for growth.
That is why we adopted a policy to deregulate major economic sectors such as energy and transportation, to name but a few.

March 6, 1990
The Budget
We replaced the Foreign Investment Review Agency, which does not arouse fond memories, with Investment Canada.
Our initiatives have produced results, Mr. Speaker. The economy has expanded for seven consecutive years. Our job creation rate has been the highest of all industrialized countries except Japan. The purchasing power and after-tax disposable income of Canadians increased dramatically. These are facts and figures that speak for themselves.
However, we also had to open up new opportunities for our economy, at a time when world trade is becoming global and increasingly powerful trading blocks are being formed. That is why we negotiated a free trade agreement with the U.S., which gives our products and services secure access to the richest market in the world and which will lead-the figures from independent agencies are there to prove it-to a sustained 3.5 per cent increase in our economic output. A lot of money, a lot of investment and a lot of jobs are reflected in this figure, Mr. Speaker.
I realize that many of our friends across the way will continue to drape themselves in the Maple Leaf, in order to oppose free trade. They don't know or pretend they don't know that in the past year, prospective investment has increased by more than 11 per cent, that business has been urging us to speed up elimination of tariffs and that Canadian companies are eager participants in our programs to promote sales in the United States. These are unmistakable signs, Mr. Speaker.
Obviously, when you have run the country on a hand-to-mouth basis for 15 years, it is not always easy to understand what is involved in long-term management of public finances which keeps the future in perspective. That is what we are doing. We are giving our companies and our workers the best possible tools to get ahead in a world that is becoming increasingly competitive and where no one is going to give it all to us on a silver platter.
The tax reform that will come into force next year is also a case in point. The new goods and services tax will rid us of a tax system that is obsolete, unfair and extremely harmful to the Canadian economy. It will give us a modem tax system, one that already exists in 48
countries across the globe. It is a system that, whatever people say to the contrary, will help low- and middle-income Canadians improve their lot.
The goods and services tax will help achieve three goals: reduce the deficit, stimulate the economy and make our tax system more equitable.
Mr. Speaker, we are well aware that certain measures are not very popular at first. This is to be expected when aiming for long-term benefits, and in any case, we are certainly not trying to win a popularity contest. That is not why we were elected, Mr. Speaker. We were elected to govern with a long-term perspective, in the best interests of Canadians.
The future demands that we act responsibly. First of all, we cannot afford to leave to future generations, to our children and grand-children, the debts that we ourselves incurred. We must ensure that Canadians will continue to have one of the most advanced health care systems in the world, social programs that are among the most generous of any country, and a modem education system. We must also be able to respond to the new challenges of the future, such as protecting the environment.
If we are to be successful, Mr. Speaker, we cannot wear blinkers. We must have a vision of the future and the courage to defend that vision, even at the risk of becoming unpopular.
Reducing the deficit and the national debt is not the end-all and be-all, but it is the only way to provide for a prosperous economy and a better future for Canadians. It is the only way to have the flexibility we need to make real choices. We cannot make real choices when one-third of every dollar collected by the government goes to pay off the debt. If we let this percentage increase, we may compromise our future by reducing that flexibility, thus becoming increasingly vulnerable and, in the long run, unable to maintain those programs to which I was referring and which are so much a part of our lives.
The Budget brought down by the Minister of Finance keeps us on the track of budgetary responsibility. The government will continue its expenditure control plan. We will save $7 billion over the next two years and nearly $20 billion over the next five.
March 6, 1990

We have asked Canadians to make many sacrifices in recent years. There is no easy way to reduce the deficit. We have done everything we could to keep the impact on Canadians to a minimum. We announced no new taxes in this Budget. Exempted from the expenditure control plan are all income security programs and most transfers to the provinces, especially the poorest provinces receiving these transfers.
Few programs have been eliminated or reduced. We preferred to cap growth of government spending in most areas, as a signal to the public and to the provinces which must realize that inflation, which has not yet been beaten, is no accident. It is not just a figure that appears once a year or once a month and tells us we have an inflation rate of 5 per cent, 4 per cent or 6 per cent. No, this figure happens to be the sum total of various factors produced by the provinces, the private sector, unions, government-the federal, provincial and municipal governments-when they fail to take the necessary steps to keep their spending below the rate of inflation. That is the only way we will be able to reduce and control inflation.
The government will also continue to introduce new measures to make its activities more efficient and less costly. Thus, increases in departmental operating and maintenance budgets will continue to be capped at 2 per cent until 1994-95. A meager 2 per cent, as has been the case since 1986-87.
Mr. Speaker, our message to Canadians is clear. Leadership in reducing the deficit has come, first of all, from the government, as all the figures have shown. In the years to come, we will continue to tighten our belts, as we have been doing for five years. We will be able to say, with pride-the government can often be accused of saying: Do as I say and not as I do. That is not the case, Mr. Speaker. We have set an example.
Before concluding, I would like to say a word about how my department, Consumer and Corporate Affairs Canada, intends to fulfil its mandate for fiscal responsibility.
My department is one of those which have done the most in recent years to increase productivity in the federal Public Service. My department has met all the expenditure reduction objectives set by Treasury Board. Thanks to office automation, rationalization and privat-
The Budget
ization, staff cuts of up to 30 or 35 per cent have been achieved in some services and our cost recovery policy has increased revenues by about 92 per cent since 1984. We realized that Canadian companies and Canadians could pay for some services from my department. They pay and it is normal and legitimate.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, my department's mandate is to ensure that the market operates efficiently and fairly. In that regard, we have a particular responsibility to help companies be more competitive. Therefore my department will have an important role to play in the coming years in building a strong economy which will enable our companies to stand out and benefit from the development opportunities that free trade and tax reform in particular provide us.
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, consumers for whom I am also responsible will ultimately benefit from a more competitive, more productive economy. Consumers will benefit from it in the end. It is important for Canadians because at some point all of us without exception are consumers in this country. I think that what we are doing for consumers' benefit is important.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words about the Department of Agriculture which has also done more than its fair share. Its budget for the next fiscal year has just been reduced by more than $400 million. The end of the assistance program for crop losses due to the 1988 drought and the cancellation of the policy to set the domestic price of wheat, to mention only these two, will enable us to make substantial savings.
The budget under consideration is in keeping with our fiscal responsibility commitment. We can no longer afford to come up with the kind of budgets like those where our Liberal friends would forecast a deficit of $2 billion or $3 billion and end up with $17 billion in the red. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, they would not even look twice at the expenditures and increase them by 14 or 15 per cent in all departments. This explains why we are now in such a tight fiscal situation and must tighten our belts even more to get our economy back on track. I am sure the budget of the Minister of Finance will help us achieve our objective. Canadians are in for a long and difficult period, but as members of the House it is our responsibility to make them understand that if we want to keep our country free and independent, and if Canadians want to remain proud of the social programs

March 6, 1990
The Budget
we have set up over the years, this can only be done with a budget like this one, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate my Hon. colleague's comments. I should like, however, to develop further the notion of a "vision of the future" which he raised.
Quite recently, a friend of mine mentioned that the budget of an individual, an organization, a government or a private enterprise greatly reflects the priorities of this individual or group. In a sense, it is an image of his or its soul, because the way I spend my money is indicate of the values I hold dear.
Now, when I consider this budget, I note that the Government increased by as much as 5 per cent the funding of a number of departments, including National Defence. I think it increased the funding for Intelligent Service by as much as 20 per cent. Other fundings were either limited or frozen. For instance, this budget comes down veiy hard on the old, the sick, the veterans, the young, the natives, Canadian women, and a number of regions: their funding were either frozen or allowed a limited increase. I am referring of course to the health care and education programs.
Moreover, taxes will increase, and I just wonder how the Minister can claim with such fanfare that there will be no new tax, when the Govemement has announced that the GST will be implemented in January 1991, unless of course it plans to withdraw it, which would be very good news for Canadian men and women.
My question to the Minister is this: If you followed my argument don't you think that serious self-examination is in order for the Government when it claims that its priorities are really what Canadian men and women need?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I want to touch briefly on interest rates, the deficit and the debt, plus an area that I am responsible for as critic for my party, namely, veterans affairs. I apologize for not notifying the minister that I would be here to do that today. I hope he is watching in his office.
I recall in 1981-1982 when interest rates got even a little higher than they are now-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Quite a bit higher.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-hearing the members of the Official Opposition, including the present Minister of Finance, berate the then Liberal government daily about the folly and the fallacy of a high interest rate policy; the folly and the fallacy of trying to prop up the Canadian dollar.
Every time somebody wants to know what our dollar is worth compared to the U.S. dollar, it is like the old Vaudeville joke, when one lady asked the other one: "How is your husband?" the other lady said: "Compared to what?"
We have been through this before historically. The government could accomplish its same deficit reduction as proposed in the budget by dropping interest rates. Using the Minister of Finance's own projections, every 1 per cent drop cuts the deficit by $1.7 billion in year one, $2.6 in year two, $3.1 billion in year 3, and $3.5 billion in year 4. The normal spread between interest rates in the United States and Canada is around a 3.0 to 3.5 per cent rate difference. But we are running at 5 and 5.5 per cent difference now.
I do not understand this nonsense. I am just an innocent stubble-jumping prairie boy. The minister complains that he is fighting inflation, but he has raised interest rates over the past year to the point now where the Bank of Canada rate is over 13 per cent, and the rates are anywhere from 14.25 to 15 per cent on
The Budget
consumer loans or mortgage loans depending on who you go to. Since he was the one who complained vociferously when the Liberals did this, why didn't the minister arrange with the Governor of the Bank of Canada to lower interest rates by 1 per cent immediately and over the next year another 1 per cent? With that mechanism alone, he would have wiped out the deficit in four years. If it meant bringing in foreign exchange controls or pegging the dollar, fine, let's do it.
On that note, I want to say for the benefit of my hon. friend, that we did that for six years during the Second World War. We financed that entire war without any foreign investment, without any foreign capital. Canadians did it by themselves.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is only one difference, there is not a war.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Why don't we have a declaration of peace and use the same methods now as we used then? It takes courage and it takes flying in the face of the old line party conventional wisdom.
If the deficit and the debt at the end of the Second World War in early 1946 were translated into 1990 dollars, it would be half again higher than our present national debt and our deficit. Thank goodness, because we had to rebuild our entire economy, we had full employment and we wiped out those debts. By 1956-57 they were paid off. My victory bonds and Canada war savings certificates were redeemed, and the same with all other Canadians.
During the Korean War, Lester Pearson pegged interest rates and imposed foreign exchange controls. In 1959-60, John Diefenbaker did exactly the same thing. The Americans did not like it, but tough cookie. We kept inflation down and we kept a relatively high employment rate. If you really want to wipe out the national debt and bring the deficit down to zero, and if we are lucky show a surplus, you have to follow a policy of full employment. I will leave it at that.
As a veteran and one who was most honoured when asked by my previous leader and the present one to be the critic for veterans affairs, I never thought I would live to see the day that a government of any kind would attack veterans. I have been here as you have, Sir, since June, 1968. Every member of Parliament in every year since then, every political party that had representation in this House agreed, and there was never any question about it, that we will never be able to fully repay them. It

March 6, 1990
The Budget
was sacrosanct. It was not as much as we could do or should do, but it was the minimum we must do.
Now we have the obscenity of this mealy-mouthed, chiselling of our war veterans. I do not understand it.
The government in the past two months has spent $3 billion of our money to do what? To prop up the Canadian dollar. Why in God's name would it want to prop it up? Every time it keeps the Canadian dollar high, it hurts our grain sales, grain exports, livestock exports, forestry products, fisheries, potash and sulphur; you name it. That is what has got us into difficulty.
Our trade surplus is the lowest it has been for God knows how long. But imagine. The government spent $3 billion of our money to prop up the Canadian dollar. Frankly, if it is at 83 or 84 cents right now, I would say put it down to about 75 cents compared to the American dollar. That would be a neat way to compete with the Americans on their export enhancement program on agricultural products and how they have been doing us out of markets on grain sales because all those international contracts are in U.S. dollars. Then we would show them where the bear sat on the buckbrush.
The fact is that one of the items to reduce the deficit picks on veterans. I did not even think a hard-hearted Tory like my hon. friend across the way would stoop that low. I just did not believe any of them would do that.
The Department of Veterans Affairs will raise rates for board and lodging for veterans in department controlled beds in long-term care and the heavy housekeeping component of the veterans' independence program will be cancelled. If this country and this government are that hard up and that desperate that they have to pick on our veterans, there is something wrong with our priorities, particularly the priorities of the government.
There is a means test on whether or not veterans will pay board and lodging in a government operated veterans home or a home operated by a provincial institution or a private institution. If a veteran who receives $820 a month of $9,840 a year, is paying no board and lodging, as
long as he is not a victim of war wounds he will have it go from zero to $240 this year. Next year it will go to $420.
Do you realize, Sir, that that incomes test is $2,000 a year below the poverty line? As a minimum criterion the incomes test should be no less than the poverty line and it should go up each year according to inflation.
Under the incomes test a married veteran will get $1,234 a year which he is allowed. That comes to $15,808. The poverty level for a married couple in Canada is $19,250. The income test for the married veteran who requires long-term care is $4,000 a year below the poverty line.
There have been remarks made both inside the Chamber and outside the Chamber. I want to express my extreme sadness. One noted and honourable spokesman for a veterans organization in Canada said the other night on television that some of these guys even leave a an estate when they die.
Is that not terrible? Is it not terrible that they were able to put away a few dollars to leave something for their children and the grandchildren? What the devil is wrong with that? We encourage every other Canadian to do it. We give them tax breaks to do it, but we do not do it for veterans. My goodness, if they are going to leave an estate, that is not terrible. They should be allowed to leave that.
The married veteran in long-term care is allowed $1,057 a month if his spouse is at home. There is a comfort allowance for him and his spouse of $128 a month. This is under the old Tory incomes test. Next year the pensions will be indexed upward by 5 per cent, but the board and lodging rates rise as well. Why bother with the increase in either one? The married veterans will still be allowed their $1,057 a month and their comfort allowance, if you can call that comfort, will remain at $128.
What cuts are involved? This year the board and lodging rates go from zero to $240 for about 1,300 veterans and lesser amounts for a larger number. Next year they go to $420 a month based on the rate of the lowest province in Canada which at the moment happens to be Alberta. It is a way for a province to be encouraged to pick up some extra money and raise its rates, which
March 6, 1990

will immediately raise the board and lodging rates veterans have to pay. There is no maximum. That $240 and $420 are not maximums.
The government deleted the heavy house cleaning allowance. It was twice a year. Even if they cut it down to once it would be all right. All of us can remember when our mothers house cleaned in the spring and fall.
The whole family had to pitch in and work. My dad washed the ceilings. The kids had to clean up the basement and wash walls. We all had to do it. But how is a 70 year old or 80 year old veteran who wants to stay out of long-term home care supposed to do that heavy house cleaning? The government kept the light house cleaning. He or his spouse could do some of that, or perhaps both, or get the kids in to help. When it comes to washing walls and ceilings, I do not want to see an 80 year old veteran trying to get up a ladder to wash a ceiling.
Then there is cleaning the drapes. Have you ever sent drapes to a diy cleaner? Dry cleaning is eliminated too. If you do your drapes once a year you know what the bill is like. Also cleaning attics, basements, garages and/or outbuildings. By the way, would you believe there are still places in Canada where they have certain kinds of outbuildings; some are one holers and some are two holers. Any home improvements, including stripping and sanding of floors, replacing and laying new carpet and chimney cleaning. Do you want to see a veteran in his seventies trying to clean his own chimney?
Good God, what are they doing? What do they think they are doing? Better still, why do they not think about what they are doing?
All parties and every member of this House since 1945 have said and agreed that we could never fully repay them. How come this government and this Parliament are going quietly-a lot of other members and I are not going to be quiet-to acquiesce to this kind of cheap chiselling on people whom we have agreed for five decades we can never fully repay? What in God's name is the government doing?
I have a document that was sent to the Regional Director General of Operations of the Pacific in Vancouver. I do not blame civil servants; they have their orders to implement government policy. When veterans have called and said "well, how come you did not tell us
The Budget
before", they have said it was because they did not know it was in the budget. There was no advance warning.
I want to conclude by referring to the increases. Yesterday the minister tried to say there were no cuts. I sent my cat to the vet the other day and we got him cut. I can tell my neighbours that that cat ain't cut. No matter which way you cut it, the veterans have an increase in their board and lodging and they have a decrease in the veterans independence program. If that ain't a cut, I never saw a cut cat in my life.
This country has no business chiselling in this area. In hundreds of other places people are making over $86,000 a year and get all the benefit of the new breaks in the RRSPs. I guess them that has gets.
I want to say that we are going to make sure that every veteran in every branch of the Legion and Army, Navy and Air Force veterans all over this country knows about this. They do not have the details. We are going to give it to them, and then they can give it to this government. I hope if the government does nothing else about this stupid budget, it will at least withdraw the provisions regarding the veterans of Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to go back to a number of things my colleague spoke about. I must say that I hope his passionate plea on behalf of veterans does not go unnoticed across Canada. I think it was eloquent and certainly put forward very clearly what is being done to the veterans and the fact that this country owes them so much.
I want to go back and talk about a couple of other things he mentioned: the question of interest rates, inflation and the dollar. The government keeps saying it has to jack up the interest rate to bring down inflation.
Somehow I got mixed up. I thought really half the problem of pushing up inflation is high interest rates. I will use one example. In housing right now interest rates are at 13.5 per cent instead of the 10 per cent that the Minister of Finance promised a year ago. This means that on a $100,000 mortgage monthly payments are $250 more. That is inflation, $250 more. The person has to earn nearly $500 to have $250 in his pocket. He has got to demand $500 more in wages. That is inflation.
My feeling is that inflation is being caused by the high interest rate policy. The government can continue to jack it up to 20 per cent, but it is not going to bring down

March 6, 1990
The Budget
inflation. In fact, it is just going to continue to push it up. I would like the members comments on that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague is as usual 100 per cent correct. He is just repeating what the present Minister of Finance said to the Liberal Minister of Finance in 1981 or 1982 about high interest rates. That government of those years and this government are the architects of their own problem. The more you raise interest rates, the more you increase the deficit.
When the Minister of Finance cries about how much of the government's expenditures have to go to pay interest charges, you would think he would phone Mr. Crow and say: "We have to do something about this". Oh, no, Mr. Crow increases the interest rates and then the Minister of Finance comes in here and says: "We have a problem. We have to cut back on veterans and a whole bunch of other outfits". All he had to do was cut back interest rates. Over the next four years, by just knocking it off 1 per cent this year and another 1 per cent next year, the accumulated reduction of the deficit will hit $10 billion. What more could you want?
If foreign investors want to take their money out tell them: "Fine. Get out. Go. We will do it ourselves." We did it for six years financing a war effort, the likes of which many other countries were never able to accomplish in proportion. That is one of the key items. The government allows interest rates to go up increasing its own deficit, and then it expects us, after paying higher interest rates, to take the cut-backs that it proposes also.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask my hon. colleague a question that is not perhaps directly related to the budget but certainly is related to his deep interest in veterans affairs.
As a Korean veteran myself, I also would like to say that I notice most members in the House tend to refer to veterans as he and perhaps this is something where we should be a little more correct, too. I am sure there may be many service women who are interested in the points that he was raising.
As he was talking this afternoon, I was looking through some correspondence and happened to come across something from one of the senior members of the Korean Veterans Association. It is still very concerned that Korean veterans have not been properly recognized
by the Government of Canada. I wonder if he would care to comment on that. I would be interested in any suggestions that he has.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I take the admonition of my hon. colleague.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A friendly admonition.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A friendly admonition. She has given them to me almost weekly. I never meant anything by being forgetful and not mentioning that there were thousands of women who served loyally in the Second World War and the Korean War, between those wars and since.
It is true the veterans of the Korean War are still being short changed. There are a few others. I have tried for years to get the Government of Canada, since 1968, to recognize the veterans of the Mackenzie-Papineau Battalion of the Spanish Civil War. There is less than 200 of them left. They are all in their eighties. One of them, a good friend of mine in Regina, passed away a couple of months ago. He tried to get recognition for years.
Every response I got about them from every Minister of Veterans Affairs was: "Well they were soldiers of fortune." They did not get paid. They paid their own way over there. They were the first ones to fight the fascists. Most of them volunteered for the Canadian forces when the Second World War started, and we still do not recognize their contributions from 1936 to 1939.
Another group we still do not recognize is the merchant marine. We lost more merchant marine men than we did from the Royal Canadian Navy in the Battle of the Atlantic. I have had excuses from Ministers of Veterans Affairs ad nauseam that they were getting commercial pay. When we checked into that, their commercial pay was the same or less than what members of the Royal Canadian Navy were getting. The government still refuses to recognize them.
I say through you, Mr. Speaker, to my colleagues in the House on all sides it is about time again-and we have done it before in other instances-that we made up as well as we can for these errors of omission and commission. Let's once and for all recognize those merchant seamen, the veterans of the Spanish Civil War, and do
March 6, 1990

more for the veterans of the Korean War who are now almost to an age like me.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance said in his recent budget: "to ensure a strong economic foundation for the future we are moving forward with the broad plan that we set out in November 1984". Unfortunately, Canadians are skeptical of the ability of the government to put its own financial house in order.
On the positive side, and we are pleased to announce on the positive side, that we in the Reform Party are glad to see that Petro-Canada is finally going to be privatized, but we also wonder why it has taken six years. Business should be involved in business, and government should be involved in government. While we are pleased to see Petro-Canada being sold, we wonder why the government is going to continue to burden this operation with the bureaucratic laws of a Crown corporation and not allow it to function like any private sector company should.
We are glad to see industrial and business subsidies being cut; we advocated this last year. Of course the Chamber of Commerce and business communities in Canada were asking for the same thing. However, we do wonder why the energy sector has been singled out.
We were also glad to hear the government borrow a line from our neighbours to the south and say: "Read my lips, no new taxes", to sell this budget. However, given this budget's substance, I believe this statement either to be irresponsible at very best, or insincere at the worse.
I note that unemployment insurance premiums will be up by 18 per cent over last year, supposedly without increasing taxes. Nor can we forget that not only did the government announce in December new surtaxes, it also has brought in Bill C-62, the new GST, which is waiting to become law before the next budget.
On the negative side, Mr. Speaker, I must tell you that the budget's bottom line is what I expected from the government. I expected a deficit around last year's projection of $28 billion, although it is still $500 million higher than even that. This budget makes the assump-
The Budget
tion that last year's course was correct. I contend it was not and still is not.
I certainly was amazed that defence was not reduced because of the events in eastern Europe. Bases in my riding were bracing themselves for cuts in light of what has been going on around the world. I certainly expected foreign aid to be reduced. There were no cuts there. Cuts in projected spending are not cuts in actual spending. It is ludicrous to suggest that a 5 per cent cut on growth is a spending cut. It simply is not.
After much talk about reductions and spending cuts, program spending will in fact increase by $3.1 billion after an increase of $5.5 billion last year. Of 29 departments, 22 had their budgets actually increased. Only 7 were reduced. If we look at what occurred in these 7 departments, we will see that the Secretary of State actually increased after the non-recurring payments to Japanese Canadians are removed. Agriculture fell, but as a result of last year's budget. Actually there are only 5 of the departments which show cuts and only 2 of those 5 will show substantial cuts.
We are disappointed that the evidence is that cries over cuts are merely a reallocation of funds within and between programs to make this seem like a tough budget. We see that the budget of the Office of the Co-ordinator of the Status of Women increased by 11 per cent, the Governor General's office increased by 13 per cent, the Senate is up by 8 per cent and general operations of the government are up by 15.8 per cent.
Again it is disappointing that in this budget there are no cuts to the cabinet, to ministerial office staffs, no cuts to limousines, no slashing of parliamentary travel budgets or MPs' perks and no cuts in middle management. Again we see in this budget, sadly, no example of restraint at the top levels.
I do say again, because I do remember that in December the President of the Treasury Board announced symbolic cuts, then they decided over a weekend not to save taxpayers' money or interest payments or to reduce the deficit, but rather to sell an unpopular tax that is to come in at 7 per cent because they knew it certainly could not sell at 9 per cent.
That is one of the problems with the government's attitude toward deficit reduction. It is a reaction to some outside force, not the result of an internal conviction. Over a weekend, they miraculously found $2 billion worth of cuts to sell the GST at 7 per cent. How many years had it cost us, the taxpayers, these $2 billion? How

March 6, 1990
The Budget
much has it added to our debt? How much has it added to the interest payments this year alone? How much more is there to cut which they do not feel compelled to cut?
I will give you a fact, Mr. Speaker. For every $1 which this government could have cut in 1984 when it was voted in to do just that and continues to spend that $1 in 1990, the government has accumulated $8.58-$6 in principle and $2.58 in interest. It will add 85 cents in interest to this year's deficit, and these are all very conservative estimates.
If it did not cut that $1 again this year, it will cost Canadians at least $1 in interest next year and will have added $10 to the debt-10 times the original amount of that $1 in 1984.
This budget may not in itself include any new taxes, but it paves the way for future tax increases. This budget fails to tackle the seriousness of our deficit by eliminating non-essential spending now and their associated costs later.
That is why I believe this budget is insincere. It is the government's attempt to sell the GST once again, but this year's budget lays the groundwork for justifying raising the GST rate because spending is not cut enough.
The finance minister has been in the job for nearly six years. When he started the deficit was $38 billion. The fiscal year which we are now ending shows a deficit of $30.5 billion. Next year's forecast is for $28.5 billion. After seven years of Tory management, we will see our deficit reduced by less than $10 billion. Then suddenly, according to their projections, in four more years we are expected to believe that the deficit will be zero. Canadians can only believe the government for so long. The government can only say for so many years that the deficit will be zero in four years. To Canadians it seems as if tomorrow never comes.
If we look back to May 23, 1985, when the finance minister tabled his first budget, he predicted the deficit under several scenarios for the period ending with the 1990 fiscal year.
Under the finance minister's most optimistic scenario that he gave us for the economic growth over the first five years, the deficit would have dropped to $18 billion this year, not $28.5 billion. The growth in the economy was better than the period of his best scenario. While the economy grew by 20 per cent over this period, revenues
grew even faster. Their share of the Gross Domestic Product outpaced the minister's projection from 16 per cent to 17.5 per cent. Despite all this extra revenue did the deficit go down? No. In fact, interest rates were usually lower than expected in most years. The fact is that spending increased. It did not fall as a percentage of the economy as expected. Spending is the true culprit. This government is the guilty party by not cutting spending enough since 1984.
Just because the government has vocal opposition in this House lobbyists outside the House, most of whom are paid by the government, are fighting every dollar cut, saying what has been done is too extreme. These comments do not mean that it is too extreme. There should be a national interest and a concern for our future economic stability, more future than just looking toward the next election.
It is a shame when only the finance minister and the Treasury Board see the deficit as a serious problem and the national concern it is. Other cabinet colleagues see themselves as advocates for special interests rather than national interests. Before this budget cabinet ministers threatened if a special interest were cut, and then announced victory when it was not cut. All the cabinet should be united in deficit reduction because it is a national concern. Otherwise, how do you expect Parliament and the country to be concerned with it?
That is why every major program for which there is a special interest in cabinet is preserved, even though we cannot afford it.
The government says reducing the deficit will help reduce inflationary pressures and along with them interest rates. I agree with this statement, but only as long as government spending and taxing is such that it is geared not to spend in inflationary areas.
I have asked for a regional breakdown of revenues and expenditure to demonstrate that the government's fiscal policies could help ease inflation. Otherwise, the use of monetary policy is the equivalent of the government throwing water on the whole country to put out a fire in the furnace it is itself stoking. The government will not provide a regional breakdown for me. Either it does not have it, which is highly unlikely, or it does not want to release it, which is far more likely. Government spending must be such that it helps reduce and not fuel inflation. Unless it provides a breakdown, Canadians are left
March 6, 1990

asking this question: What are they hiding from us as Canadians, is it incompetence or inequality for the regions?
Fairness does not mean spending the most on central Canada because all things gravitate to the centre of the universe where the most votes are, incidentally, in politics. The government steadfastly refuses to show us its spending to demonstrate that it is fair.
In this budget it has been estimated that approximately 40 per cent of the cuts directly affect Alberta. Albertans are not unwilling to make sacrifices. We all know that they sacrificed a great deal in the early 1980s under the National Energy Program. There are several areas where Alberta is being hit specifically. There is the public utilities income tax transfer, OSLO and CEIP. Under the NEP and the PGRT the energy sector did suffer. Now we are seeing it happen again. Albertans are feeling apprehensive about the Minister of the Environment's new environmental agenda. Will this slap a heavy hydrocarbon tax on Alberta? Albertans do want spending cuts, but Albertans want fairness in the cuts and equality of sacrifice right across the country.
British Columbians are asking why the Polar 8 has been cancelled while none of the Canadian patrol frigates are being cancelled, especially the three subcontracted to central Canada.
Alas, neither does there seem to be any sense of fairness for the provinces selected for reductions in transfer payments. Apparently, the most fiscally responsible were selected for that. We did not see a sense of fairness four days before the budget, when no doubt the cuts had already been finalized, the minister surreptitiously agreed to voluntarily pay $90 million in payroll taxes to the Ontario government, a tax which costs the federal government $400 million annually in lost revenue. Why, in the name of fairness, did the government agree to this tax payment four days before the budget? How is this fair to Alberta and B.C., two other of the "have" provinces?
Not only do the cuts in transfer payments to the provinces raise the constitutional impropriety of the federal government legislating in areas of provincial jurisdiction, but the federal government, even with these
The Budget
reductions, continues to dictate standards without providing access to the tax base to finance the high standards demanded. Furthermore, passing the blame to the provinces simply does not solve the problem of tax increases at the provincial level or unnecessary federal government spending.
Let me deal with some of the fiscal uncertainty that this government has created by failing to reduce the deficit. It has affected interest rates and the value of the dollar. All products of the government need to borrow greater amounts for our debt. It is not the other way around. Furthermore, the government's inability to get the deficit under control has meant the competitiveness of our industry and the entrepreneurial capital of Canadians is being taxed away to pay foreign debtors and to upwardly distribute tax revenue to those Canadians who can most afford to lend money.
Since this government has been in office, the reliance on foreign debtors has more than doubled the original amount. As the government taxed more of Canadians' income and left them with less and less to reinvest in their own country, foreign capital had to substitute for the deficiency in the economy each year. To attract and pay for foreign capital, our competitiveness is hurt with the high dollar and high interest rates needed to attract these resources.
I see no recognition of this program in this budget, nor any attempt to deal with the very real problem of the government taxing away and spending away our international competitiveness to fund programs at the expense of our future competitiveness as a trading nation and our ability to compete under the free trade agreement. The finance minister stated that these are all powerful reasons for holding to the plan we started in 1984. They certainly are. But they do not explain why this government has deviated so far and long from its original plan which would have given us a deficit of $18 billion.
The government itself treats deficit reduction as a more partisan game than anyone else in this House. To its opponents it says: "You are fiscally irresponsible socialists", and then pats itself on the back and says: "Well, compared to the other guys, look what we've done". For myself, the Reform Party, many Canadians and, sadly, international observers in the financial mar-

The Budget
kets are saying: "You were in office, not your opponents, and you have not done much".
The government's words and deeds on deficit reduction do not balance, so how could its budgets?
The government should have controlled our deficits so as not to leave a huge financial burden of debt to our future generations, but it did not. Under the transfer payment changes we see a dearth of research dollars. Young people, our human capital, will get the wrong signal that they are neither important to, nor supported by, government. Surely, developing brain power and technical specialists is the best long term deficit reducer for this country. No responsible government should want to leave a legacy of economic destruction and neglect to our posterity, just as no responsible government wants to leave a legacy of an environment ravaged by our neglect. The Reform Party believes strongly that both policy outlooks are inseparable for any party which sincerely believes in responsible government.
The government's sad refusal to acknowledge its lack of progress will not help to reduce deficits, nor will its protestations to calm international markets, nor will a litany of statistics created to disguise the facts. The instability of our dollar, rumours of downgrading our bond rating and high interest rates to finance the deficit are all signs of the lack of progress.
This government is responsible for the size of the deficit. It has been in office for six years. It cannot blame the size of the deficit and level of interest payments on the previous Liberal administrations of Pierre Trudeau, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, or whoever.
The Reform Party outlined in the 1988 election the cuts that should be made to get the deficit under control, all to unnecessary programs. However, sadly, these cuts are no longer sufficient. I regret to say that it has taken too long to tackle the issue of unnecessary spending. To control the deficit now will require cuts to programs that all Canadians need, not just want.
My party has been accused of wanting to cut medicare. Nothing could be farther from the truth. Yet we have seen this government cutting millions in health and post-secondary education. Soon the question will not be: What can we afford to cut? but, desperately: What can we afford to keep? That is the state that we are in.
Health and post-secondary education are what we need to keep, not cut. Even under the finance minister's current projections, which are optimistic at best, interest payments will just level off. The projections after two years are in fact a fantasyland of projections, low future interest rates, low unemployment and high economic growth which this budget does little to build the fiscal foundations for.
This government is leading us to the brink of economic ruin proclaiming: "We have been doing a great job". But the international community knows otherwise, and Canadians know otherwise. All the signs are there for nervousness.
Earlier this afternoon the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs said: "Canadians say, Cut, cut, cut, but don't cut in my backyard". We are at the point in Canada now where in my home province of Alberta people are saying: "We are willing, personally, to take cuts". Sadly enough, the cabinet ministers themselves are saying in reaction to the gathering storm clouds of economic warning: "It's all perception, the problems out there. I'll be hanged if you will cut spending on my particular program and I'll be hanged if I'll be hanged". Unfortunately, perception aside, reality lies in front of us. Reality lies ahead. This country will be hanged if they don't.
Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External
Affairs): Mr. Speaker, that must be the vaguest speech that has been made in this budget debate.
I was interested in the hon. member's references to sincerity. Of course the test of sincerity is whether she is prepared to back up her rhetoric with an indication of particular areas in which she will cut. She indicated that she did not think there had been cuts enough in agriculture. I wonder if she will tell us what programs in agriculture she thinks should be cut.
I would also be interested in her responding to this very simple question. Does she support the continuation of the OSLO project? Does she support the continuation of the Polar S?

March 6, 1990

First, I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, and make it public to the House, that we issued a press release from my office last year saying what cuts we thought could be made. I also have to say that I received a personal phone call from staff of the senior minister. He certainly knows some areas in which the Reform Party and I personally have advocated cutting. I have been accused of having simplistic answers to budget control. I know there are no easy answers to budget control. I stand sometimes on a lonely road on this side of the House, but I certainly am willing to do that. That is positive. I am glad to give credit where credit is due.
We have had meetings both privately and publicly with people about the OSLO project. They are in the vein that it is unfortunate because the prices are so low now. What I did say about the Polar 8 is that maybe there is no need for the Polar 8 as the government thinks. What I was discussing was the apparent discrepancy for the people in B.C. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as always the privilege is mine on behalf of my Nepean constituents to participate in debate here in the House of Commons on this particular occasion and of course on the budget.
During the House break this past week I had the opportunity to speak to many of my constituents and discuss the effects of the various budget measures being imposed by the present government.
Despite what the finance minister has relayed to the people of Canada, this budget is full of tax increases. This budget will relentlessly pursue a brutal and discriminatory high interest rate policy. It will widen the gap between the rich and poor. It will respectively end regional development in Canada as Canadians have
known it. The fallacy of no new tax is the most blatant act of deception.
This government has lost the vision of this country, or maybe it has never realized what Canada is all about.
This budget indicates that the government has no sense of responsibility for the framework of Canada as we know it today.
Let us look at a few areas. First, the government has not made any significant moves to cut its own spending. Let us take a look at one area, the PMO.
When the Liberals left office in 1984 the cost of the PMO was $6 million and there were 104 person years of employment. Upon taking office the new Prime Minister increased the budget of the PMO by close to $1 million and added 16 more person years.
What is happening today in 1990? We tried to find out what the figures were today. Unfortunately, we are now not able to get a clear idea of how much the PMO has increased staff and spending this year because they have come up with another new accounting trick to hide the number of people on staff. The PMO has decided to eliminate all political staff from the accounting in the 1990-91 Estimates so that the person years of the PMO are listed as nil. This trickery is a blatant attempt to hide how much the PMO is costing Canadians and how many more people are now employed by the Prime Minister to figure out more ways to trick Canadians.
Federal funding for universities through transfers to the provinces, since 1983 has been cut by $8.9 billion. The 1990 budget cuts alone for health care and education are a reduction of $7.3 billion in payments to the provinces. Yet the minister has never consulted with anyone to determine the effects of these drastic measures.
Funding for post-secondary education should not be seen as an expenditure. Education is an investment, a necessary investment in Canada's future.
Has the government looked at the damaging effects the reduction in research and development funding will have? By passing the responsibility for funding and performing R and D to the private sector Canada runs the risk of jeopardizing long term scientific commitments.
March 6, 1990

Some $39 million is cut from planned science programs at a time when Canada desperately needs to be increasing science-based innovation to ensure our economic strength in the future.
The social housing budget in the next five years will be reduced by $165 million. This is at a time when the homeless in Canada number 200,000, or 1 per cent of our population. In addition, the GST will cause new house prices and renovated home costs to increase.
The most callous of budget cuts is to our veterans. How can the Minister of Veterans Affairs say, and I quote: "The budget will have a minor impact on veterans"? The long term care costs to Canada's veterans will be increased by $35 million. Does this government have any conscience at all?
Women's programs will be seriously affected. Budget cuts to core financing for 80 women's centres across the country will most likely see many of them close. Many of these service women in rural areas. These agencies act as referral centres for women on issues of friendship, native groups and battered women. They provide essential services to women at a time when violence is being recognized as one of the most pernicious forms of behaviour against women.
Cuts in social housing will affect women. The majority of poor women in this country are single mothers.
Once again, corporations get off easy in respect of the corporate income tax. In the 1990-91 fiscal year the federal government is expected to collect $2.4 billion less than predicted a year ago. Had the government collected what it expected from corporations, it would not have had to cut its expenditures by $2.8 billion this year in its budget.
Astonishingly, though, when the business sector is so adamant about deficit reduction, the minister has chosen to lighten the burden of corporate taxation since the Conservatives came into power. Whereas corporate taxes accounted for 13.2 per cent of total federal revenues in 1984 and 1985, in 1990-91 corporate taxes will account for only 10.4 per cent of federal revenues. Who is picking up the slack in between? It is being picked up by the low income and the middle-income person.
This projected trend is all the more difficult to comprehend, given that the corporate sector will be a major beneficiary of substituting the GST for the MST. Even assuming that removing the FST is fully passed
The Budget
forward to consumers, the corporate sector will still save some $6 billion in taxes on goods and services. Further, in 1991-92 manufacturers will be refunded more than $2 billion for the FST paid on inventories. Stage two of tax reform is veiy beneficial for the corporate sector.
One of the most incredible deficiencies in the budget is one that does not affect my ratepayers, but it does affect the national economy, in particular the Atlantic economy. There is no new money in the budget to address the fisheries crisis in Atlantic Canada. I say, shame on you on the government side of the House. This is a region of Canada that is so dependent on this industry.
Since this government came to power in 1984 unprecedented revenues-over $120 billion in six years-were realized through economic growth. Yet for a government which insists it is interested in deficit reduction, it certainly missed the opportunity to make meaningful reductions in the deficit during those years when we were experiencing world-wide economic growth. What did it do with this 70 per cent revenue growth? What was the $120 billion used for? We do not know, and the government is not telling. It certainly was not for deficit reduction.
Canadians across this country are fed up with this government and its practice of raising taxes-33 times in five years. Yet it has not reduced its own costs. Revenues can be raised by means other than a GST, Canadians are saying. Scrap the tax and let us get down to the basics of running this country, and running it the way it should be run.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the excellent speech made by my colleague. She certainly covered a lot of ground in a very short time. I commend her on the conciseness and the punch it contained in such a short time.
I want to comment on that part of her presentation in which she said that the most callous of all cuts were the cuts made to veterans. I find it singularly distracting and somewhat disappointing, if not incredible, that in discussing this in Question Period with the Minister of Veterans Affairs two days in as row the minister has said that there are no cuts. I am having a lot of trouble with that. Obviously, veterans organizations are as well because I, as the veterans affairs critic, am getting an awful lot of comment and reaction from one end of the country to the other. Veterans cannot understand how a minister

The Budget
can say there are no cuts and on the other hand they are losing a total of $35 million.
I note in a book authored by the President of the Treasury Board entitled Managing Government Expenditures that it talks about savings of $8 million and $10 million in the period 1990-91 will be obtained under the Veterans Independence Program which is designed to keep the veterans at home so they do not have to go to hospitals. By restricting the range of services that are funded, this is how this $18 million will be saved.
I think the important thing to remember here is that the average of a Canadian veteran is 70. This cut-back on the Veterans Independence Program which involves heavy housekeeping is very important to them if the aim of the program is to be upheld.
I commend my colleague on her use of the term callous. I can only hope that the comments by my colleagues, other people on this side of the House and perhaps even some on the government side of the House about the callousness of this particular cut will make the Minister of Veterans Affairs see fit to go back either to the Prime Minister or to the Minister of Finance to see if he can make some amelioriation or some adjustment to restore this benefit that has been taken away from veterans. This is the first time since the Great Depression that anything has been taken from veterans.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague and comment on his remarks. I think the old saying goes that if you repeat a story often enough you begin to believe that what you are saying is true. I am beginning to think that the minister responsible for veterans affairs has repeated to himself and to his colleagues often enough that there are no cuts to the veterans in this country that he himself is beginning to believe it. That is unfortunate because I know that there are cuts. Those veterans know that there are cuts.
I wonder how many people in this House of Commons have visited a veteran in a veterans' home in their area. The one here in Ottawa is called the Rideau Veterans' Home and is on Alta Vista Drive. I would invite you to go and visit a veteran and to see the accommodation for the ones who are in the home where we are increasing then-charges in this home. Sure, less than $300 a month is paltry for the government. They think this is a minor inconvenience. But to those veterans who are living on a
very limited pension it is a major expenditure for them. It is not so much for the ones who are living in the home, but the ones who are able to live in their own homes and are now going to lose their housekeeping funding money that was being provided to them before when they cannot get out and shovel their driveway, clean their windows or do the basic necessities that you and I can do because we are still able-bodied people. Again I say, shame on this government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to address some of the problems facing Prince Edward Island and, in particular, my riding of Cardigan.
My riding is predominantly rural, made up mostly of farmers, fishermen and small businessmen. Most of the employment in the area is seasonal, and as a result UIC benefits are extremely important. With so much seasonal employment in P.E.I., it is necessary to find a way to reduce our reliance on unemployment insurance. One program, the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, known as ACOA, was established to create more longterm, stable employment. However, the 1989-1990 and the 1990-1991 budgets have done much to reduce the effectiveness of this program.
Last year the budget of the Minister of Finance cut a large chunk out of the ACOA budget. And if that was not bad enough, this year all grants for the program have been completely eliminated. This, in effect, has reduced ACOA to a simple bank, nothing more. The purpose of ACOA was to attract business through incentives. Now that these incentives no longer exist, business interest in the program is on a decline, dramatically.
Prior to the budget, the government promised aid to the Atlantic fishery in this, its time of crisis. Many references were made to the need for substantial aid to the area, the same as was given to the western grain growers. However, as we now know, the budget contained nothing for the fisheries industry. This gives a clear and unequivocal signal to Atlantic Canadians that the Prime Minister and the government he leads do not consider the fisheries crisis a priority. Otherwise, the

government would have acted as quickly as it did in the western grain crisis.
Within the next six months, the P.E.I. fishery could find itself in a crisis situation, just like that occurring in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. The recent U.S. legislation restricting lobsters under 3.25 inches will cause irreparable damage to the island fishery and economy. This legislation will affect 80 per cent of our lobster exports to the U.S. market. The impact is enormous, considering the lobster industry employs 10 per cent of my province's labour force. It represents 80 per cent of the Island fishery and accounts for 25 per cent of the Island's exports. In essence, the province's second largest industry is on the verge of collapse, should negotiations to repeal the law be unsuccessful.
The problems in the fishery on the Island do not stop there. Nearly every month I receive letters from local fishermen alerting me that yet another wharf or harbour is badly in need of upgrading or repairs. These small craft harbours are vital to the long-term viability of the Island fishery and, therefore, must remain, at a minimum, operable.
It has been noted by many industry officials that the current small craft harbour budget is ridiculously insufficient to meet the current needs. The recent budget cut of $4 million to this program illustrates this government's failure to recognize the gravity of this very serious situation.
Several years ago my riding of Cardigan was held by the Hon. Dan MacDonald, an outstanding Canadian war veteran who lost both an arm and a leg defending Canada in World War II. He represented Cardigan and Prince Edward Island with great distinction. With Dan as Minister of Veterans Affairs, the department developed a more human touch because he was aware of the veterans' needs, for he also was a veteran.
It is very sad to see the damage that six years of Tory government can bring. More than 5,000 aging veterans, who by illness or injury are confined to chronic care hospitals will now have to pay more than $3,000 each for their beds. This is a slap in the face to all veterans across Canada. This government has clearly lost all semblance of humanity, the most recent example being the regret-
The Budget
table action against our war veterans. Veterans should be treasured, not destroyed, most Canadians would surely agree with me on this point.
During the last six years, the government has not dealt sufficiently with the question of post-secondary education. Recently the government has stressed that the need for an educated labour force and better training. Therefore, WOUld it not make more sense to provide these institutions which train and educate, with more financial assistance to meet these goals? Instead of increasing financing to post-secondary institutions, the government saw fit to cut the Established Programs Financing.
In effect, this will force students in Prince Edward Island's only university and only college to pay more for their education. Prince Edward Island is in a depressed region, and currently over 75 per cent of all Island university students must take out loans to support their education. The budget will certainly make this figure rise. In light of this, this government's commitment to education and training is certainly in shambles.
The cuts to Established Programs Financing will also affect the ability of the health care system to perform at its present level. To maintain its present level of service in the health field, the provincial government must increase taxes. This would certainly seem to contradict the minister's statement of "no new taxes".
The flip side of this is that if taxes are not increased, then the level of service must be reduced. Could this be the beginning of harmonizing our Canadian and American health systems, to put Canadians on the same level as the American health system? The people of Cardigan certainly hope not. We know, and the government knows, that Islanders and all Canadians will not permit this attack on our medical system.
I would like to turn my attention to the Prince Edward Island tourist industry. Each year Prince Edward Island attracts 800,000 visitors. They come to watch Anne of Green Gables and other performances at Confederation Centre of the Arts. They come to see the beautiful scenery and historic buildings such as Province House known as the birthplace of Canada. Of course, visitors come to enjoy beautiful beaches, excellent seafood and our fine P.E.I. potatoes. Our tourist industry could take a severe plunge in fortunes, beginning this year, when the

March 6, 1990
The Budget
tourist season goes through its first year with the devastating VTA Rail cuts in effect.
Also, it has been predicted that nationally, 30,000 jobs will be lost as a result of the government's infamous GST. In Atlantic Canada, with about 10 per cent of Canada's population, that translates to about 3,000 jobs. The Tourist Industry Association of Prince Edward Island has formally denounced the GST as being potentially disastrous for the industry in Atlantic Canada.
The GST will do two things for certain. It will increase taxes, and it will cause the loss of thousands of jobs, not only in Cardigan, not only in Prince Edward Island but all across Canada. This is something of which the government should surely be ashamed.
Finally, I wish to thank you for the time to express, through me, the views of the people of Cardigan of this budget.

I want to review with him a number of the difficulties that his province has experienced. Perhaps he could tell me which one has had the most disastrous effect on this small Island.
The closing of the military, of course, was one that has caused great anxiety among the people of Prince Edward Island.
He referred not only to the current fishing difficulties, but those that he anticipates. He also made reference to the budgetary implications, the reductions for the veterans and how badly we and many other Canadians feel that they have been mistreated. He also referred to health reductions that will have an impact upon the elderly and those who are not well, as well as the reductions in education which will have an impact upon our young people who are seeking to build a better future for themselves, the province and country.
I have also been told that these reductions are now having some negative effects upon the elementary and secondary sectors, particularly of small provinces, because they do not have the funds to try to keep the health and post-secondary infrastructures that are already in place.
Finally, the hon. member mentioned tourism and the impact the goods and services tax will have on that, quite apart from the increased taxation that will result because of the reductions to health and education. I would ask him to comment on those measures he believes have had the most disastrous and negative effect on the people of his constituency of Cardigan, or on the province itself?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would think that probably what would have the most devastating effect in my area is if this law passed by the U.S. is allowed to remain in place. If we cannot get this law that restricts lobster under 3-1/4 inches from entering the U.S. market, it will be disastrous for the fishermen in Cardigan.
There is no question that the reduction of funds to health and education and the loss of our military base have removed dollars from Prince Edward Island and the Island economy, but with this this move in fisheries, it will be totally devastating to our fishing industry.
There are many other problems, of course. With cuts to small craft harbours, we now have many harbours all around the Cardigan that is desperately in need to repair. But if we cannot sell the fish, it will be a disastrous decision, so we hope to God the free trade panel will do some good.
