speakeroldname: Mrs. Dorothy Dobbie (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to endorse the over-all thrust of this budget. It is a responsible budget. It is a sensitive budget, and it is a budget that is geared to the realities of today and Canada's position in a competitive global market-place. It is a budget that seeks intelligent compromise and balance between sound money management and the demands of a society which

has learned the addictive art of constant gratification. This is a budget that imposes restraint but it is not a budget that bruises or punishes.
Some hon. members opposite will disagree. Lacking real targets for criticism, they will seek shadowy targets, bogeymen with which to frighten the public. But this budget contains no bogeymen. Even so, we heard a moment ago and we will continue to hear impassioned speeches about how the federal government has transferred its problems on to the backs of the provinces.
Some will complain that the provinces will be forced to cope by cutting, spending or by raising taxes. No doubt, that is true. No matter how you slice it, every dollar that we spend as governments, whether we are the federal government or the provincial government or the municipal government, comes out of the very same pocket, yours and mine and the fellow across the way.
But worse, and in my opinion far worse, is that every dollar that we spend beyond our ability to pay comes out of those same pockets, but not just on what we have earned today but on what we will earn tomorrow and what our children will earn and, if we keep it up at the same pace, what our grandchildren will earn.
There is no magic bottomless pitcher here spewing forth money in an endless stream. There is only you, me and these hon. members across the way, and what we can produce from the sweat of our labours. Whether it is the federal government, provincial government or the municipal government, we all have an equal responsibility to curb spending and manage the taxpayers' dollar more efficiently.
To suggest somehow that the movement of the tax burden from one level of government to the other will somehow affect the bottom line, what you and I pay as individuals and as taxpayers, is sheer nonsense. No matter who spends, no matter what level of government spends, the same guys pay, you and I and the fellow next door.
Currently, 35 cents out of every federal dollar that the federal government collects goes to service the debt. Only 12 cents of the provincial tax dollar goes for the same purpose. Does it make sense for Canada to borrow even more money to pass on to the provinces? Is that not just a shell game, like we have heard? Does the freeze on the established funding program not simply expose that
The Budget
shell game? The expenditure reductions announced in this budget are absolutely vital to Canada's future.
Let us just take a look at our country from a broader point of view for the moment. Those of us who have done business abroad or who have travelled abroad have come to realize that Canada has been living in a dream world for the past couple of decades. We have lost touch with that stark reality of life that is there for most of the world's population. That reality is that you have to work for what you get and you cannot live forever beyond your ability to produce. Sometime, someone has to pay the piper and that time is now.
We are indeed a rich nation, richer beyond the wildest dreams of many, but even Canada cannot afford to spend without regard for the future because we must ultimately pay for that kind of philosophy, and to do so we are forced to rely on other countries, countries who manage their resources more successfully than we do.
Let us just ask ourselves why these countries are prepared to lend us their savings. Is it because we are nice guys, because we are good people? I am afraid not. There are simple economic reasons. Foreign lenders give us money to cover our profligate spending because they can make money on their investment. It costs us plenty to borrow. The cost of this borrowing robs us of our ability to pay for the things that will add to our wealth, that will enhance our competitive position tomorrow. That is the position that we have lost through the tremendous tax burden that we place on our citizens and on our business community.
Mr. Speaker, do not believe for a moment that even these money markets are willing to fund us indefinitely. In fact, insecurity about Canada's economy has prompted comment from the international monetary people in the past. The message is straightforward and clear cut: Get your fiscal house in order; stop spending beyond your means.
What does that mean to us? It means that if we refuse to listen, if we fail to take exactly the kind of measures that have been announced here in this House on February 20 by the Minister of Finance, then we can expect continued pressure on our interest rates, we can expect an erosion of confidence in Canada as a good place to invest. We can expect a reduction of confidence in Canada as a mature responsible nation which has
i

March 6, 1990
The Budget
earned a right at the decision-making tables when international affairs are being discussed.
Today no country can afford to live in isolation. What we do, even in our internal affairs will have an international impact. That in turn will impact upon us. We must learn to co-exist in a market driven society prepared to respond to the subtle checks and balances that are a natural part of that system. We must have the flexibility as well to respond to international conditions as they shift and change, as they are shifting and changing even now. But a country so deeply in debt that more than one-third of its tax revenue goes into servicing this debt, cannot have this flexibility and the freedom to do these things. A country that has mortgaged its future cannot possibly be in total control of that future.
Mr. Speaker, is that the kind of country that Canadians want? I think not. We pride ourselves on being in command of our future and some claim indeed that the 21st century belongs to Canada. But that is difficult to believe when it looks like we could enter the 21st century in hock up to our necks.
In fact, unless we take hold, unless we take strong, fearless measures to reduce our debt we could enter that century bankrupt. A nation's strength and autonomy is based on its wealth. Without financial resources a country is weak and vulnerable, defenceless against foreign incursions of all kinds. Being broke is one thing, being heavily in debt is quite another, because when you are in debt your vulnerability becomes public property. Everybody knows that you are in trouble. But some will argue that Canada has always been in debt. We built our nation on the debt incurred to build the railway, they will say. But I say there is a vast difference between a fledgling nation borrowing to build its infrastructure and a mature country borrowing because it cannot manage its vast resources and live within its means.
We hear a great deal about our social programs and every move toward sensible money management is held up as a deadly threat toward these programs. Let us examine the issue in the clear pure light of reason. First of all, why do we have social programs? Well, the answer is simple. Social programs are a natural emanation of an
enlightened society's will to deal with an innate fact, the innate fact of inequality. Our social order compels us to provide sustenance and assistance to members of the group who cannot temporarily or permanently provide for themselves. I do not think many people would disagree with this basic philosophy.
Where the quarrel begins is over when this assistance should actually kick in. Should we be giving social assistance to the middle class? When I was a young girl, taking any form of social assistance was something to be avoided at all costs. Today it seems that things are different. We have taken the basic premise of social assistance to a point that it is not only potentially harmful but is also beyond what we can afford to support in many cases. We have done this in the mistaken belief that there is some unlimited source of income to be tapped for this.
Well, there is not. The government's only source of income is you and me. It is not true that you can tax the corporations, tax the rich, tax the tax avoiders, and somehow suddenly solve the fiscal shortfall. Indeed, Canada has already taxed corporations to a level that is bordering on the uncompetitive, and to increase the pressure simply forces companies, Canadian companies along with others, to move their assets elsewhere.
Some members opposite will not like to hear this but business is in fact our only source of wealth in the kind of society that we have in place today, and business is highly mobile. If conditions in a certain jurisdiction are unbalanced, unfavourable, business simply picks up and moves on and so does personal wealth.
Look at what has been happening in China and in Hong Kong. Ever since it became clear that the People's Republic of China would take over Hong Kong in 1997, large corporations and the wealthy have been quietly hedging their bets, setting up conduits through which they can move their capital quickly and efficiently if things get tough. Well, much of that money has already moved to Canada because Canada has been seen as a stable economy under a not-too-restrictive government with a reasonable monetary policy. But all we have to do is tighten the screws on that policy through heavier regulation and taxation and just watch that capital leave the country seeking a more favourable climate.

March 6, 1990

So tax the rich, tax the corporations more, tax the tax avoiders if you can catch them-the net is so tight in Canada right now that very little escapes. In the end what do you have for this exercise? Ultimately, probably less than you have today because you have driven the wealth producers out of the country.
The answer is balance. We must accept that there are some things that we cannot afford. We must accept that there is a need to better manage the resources that we have. We must accept that a balance has to be struck, and in fact balance is what the minister has sought and has achieved in his monetary policy since 1984. Balance is what I believe the minister has achieved in this budget.
Let us look at the budget for a moment. What does it really do? Well, for one thing it does not raise taxes and that is very good news for a citizenry that has been feeling squeezed by several levels of government. So no new taxes. No additional taxes is another step in my opinion in freeing up choices for Canadians. The goods and services tax which replaces a pernicious tax on manufactured goods is the first step in that exercise.
Next, the budget reduces spending through programs of restraint across the board. Social programs are not affected and in fact services have received actual dollar increases.
The Opposition has zeroed in on the transfers to provinces. Opposition members claim that the freeze on the Established Programs Funding will somehow lead to the total collapse of the Canadian education and health systems. Both are matters of provincial jurisdiction so that takes quite a leap in logic.
Provinces will not get less than they get right now. In fact, the have-not provinces like those in the Atlantic region or Manitoba will continue to receive dollar increases in line with the growth in the economy over the next two years through the equalization transfers. It should also be noted that since 1977 provinces have made their own decisions over how their established programs funding is spent. I repeat, provinces can use their EPF transfers which were originally earmarked for health and post-secondary education in any way they see fit. If health care and post-secondary education in Canada are suffering, perhaps provincial governments
The Budget
would like to examine their own spending priorities or reorganize the way they manage their budgets.
What else is in this budget? More good news. Grants to businesses will be reduced and replaced by repayable loans. Businesses themselves have been suggesting this, and why? Well, because grants and subsidies distort the market-place and contribute to a dependent, non selfsustaining commercial infrastructure that undermines the integrity of our economy. The government is getting out of business. This is excellent news.
Significantly, Petro-Canada will be sold, transferring state control to the hands of the public and repeating the remarkable success story of the Air Canada sale. It is right to sell Petro-Canada to Canadians as individuals. It is wrong for the state to control such an important conglomerate and to acquire its control through the use of tax dollars. State-owned, state-controlled businesses present an element of unfair competition to natural enterprise. They tend also to be inefficient, or dictatorial or both because they do not have to depend on the vagaries of the market-place and respond.
Since its incorporation in 1975, Petro-Canada has grown into a multi-faceted giant whose tentacles extend into many areas that are generally very well served by the private sector. So it is time to return the assets of Petro-Canada to the people who, as individuals with market-driven incentives, will manage those assets far better than can government. In addition, funds raised through the sale of shares can assist the newly emerging, commercially-owned Canadian company to capitalize purchases to keep it appropriately competitive with international interests.
The government is also selling Telesat Canada and winding up the affairs of a number of other Crown corporations that have outlived their usefulness or their original purpose.
The government has also addressed its spending right here at home. Today the civil service is at the same manpower level it was at in 1973 and wage restraint continues to be the order of day with federal public sector increases running at about 3.5 per cent, well below the cost of living. The government has closed tax loopholes.
The government continues to wage war on waste and redundancies. Since 1987-88, the government has been running an operating surplus which now stands at $9 billion. This is a clear indication that the fiscal policies of

March 6, 1990
The Budget
the Minister of Finance are working. Whether my hon. opponent likes to admit it or not, they are working.
I have to conclude by saying that this budget is a prudent budget and it is a sensitive budget. It recognizes Canada's conceits and respects them, but it is a budget that nurtures the disadvantaged while spurring on the strong and the enterprising. The hon. minister has done a wonderful job in trodding a delicate line toward a goal of a stronger Canada. I commend his efforts and I applaud his courage. He has done what is right over what is expedient.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw to the member's attention a couple of things she certainly has not talked about. In my community of Surrey North, which is the fastest-growing community in Canada, there are problems. One of them is housing and the affordability of it. I would like her to set out for me clearly what things in this budget are going to help the affordability of housing. What things are going to bring down the interest rate by 5 or 6 per cent, which is necessary to get housing under control?
What about the fact that the social housing program has been totally gutted? CMHC has now been turned into an agency that is nothing more than an insurance broker for the private sector. The Conservatives have totally abandoned any concept of affordability in housing, any concept that the country has a responsibility to provide housing for people on middle or low incomes. They are simply concerned about making sure that those friends of theirs who wish to flip property for massive profits are able to do so.
Second, she says there is no harm in this budget. In my municipality we have a 400-bed shortage in hospitals. Some of the existing beds are not being opened simply because there are not enough operating funds. Since 1971 we have gone backwards in terms of the ratio of hospital beds to population. The provincial government is not, with a cutback from the federal government, going to increase its funding. It is having enough difficulty maintaining its funding. It is simply not going to come up with the additional dollars. It is a federal government
responsibility to ensure that there is universal health care in this country.
I would like her to comment on those two things. What are the positives in this budget to assist families, firsttime home buyers to obtain affordable housing? Second, try to explain to me and to the people of British Columbia why this is not going to be a blow to our serious health care crisis in the province.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his multi-faceted question. First of all, the tone of his question suggests that he believes in that myth that I was speaking about earlier, that somehow money grows on trees, that if you take the dollar that we collect as a tax collector, by splitting it into three pieces like many fishes, you can make it grow into something beyond what it is.
In fact, it makes no difference whether the dollar is coming from the federal government or the provincial government or the municipal government, it is all coming from you. When you ask what the government has done to do this, that and the other thing to assist this person and that person, the fact is we are taking the dollars out of your pocket and we are cutting them up as governments and telling you how your dollars should be spent. The hon. member may feel that that is appropriate where he comes from, but there are many Canadians who not only do not feel it is appropriate, they simply cannot afford to have it done anymore. When 50 or 60 cents of your wages come out of your pocket and go into taxes you have to have some concerns.
Second, the hon. member asked about housing. He says that the government has abandoned a lot of programs that had to do with assisting first-time home buyers and so on. He is quite correct in that. The government is abandoning a number of assistance programs for middle-class people under the expectation that Canadians are strong enough, that they are confident enough and that they have the ability to fend for themselves, just as they did when I was a girl growing up. They have just stopped learning to do that in the last couple of decades when a philosophy prevailed in this country that somehow you could get something for nothing.
You cannot get something for nothing in this world. You can only put off paying what you owe today until tomorrow. The hon. member is suggesting that somehow we should put off until tomorrow paying what we owe today, what we owe for yesterday and what we owe for

the day before because somebody else did a lot of profligate spending. Already our children are in debt up to their necks because of that kind of philosophy. If we keep it up our grandchildren will be in debt up to their necks and there will not be a country called Canada because we will not have the strength, the ability or the resources to be able to command our own future.
I would suggest that if it is true, as the hon. member says, that there are people waiting in line for hospital beds in his province of British Columbia, perhaps the provincial government should take a look at how those hospital beds are being funded and find more creative and more productive ways of seeing that the health needs of the population are met. Clearly, the way governments are doing it right now and the way governments have been doing it for the last little while, has not been working. We are spending more and the services are getting less. There must be another alternative. I do not think the reasonable alternative is to take taxpayers' dollars and turn them over to bureaucracy and suppose that all our problems are going to be magically solved.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should listen to what he just said. He suggested that somehow we are taking from the poor and giving to the rich. I am not sure how he works that out. will not have any resources. You cannot take from the poor to give to the rich. The poor have no resources. It is a silly question.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been in the House for most of the day. To say that some of the speeches I have heard today are incredible is putting it mildly. The speech of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, the parliamentary secretary, is a case in point. I could go into that in detail, but there was another one that was even more unbelievable, and that was made by the Minister of Supply and Services earlier today.
I would like to deal with some of the points he raised in his attempts to defend this disastrous budget that the Minister of Finance has imposed on Canadians. He had the gall, and I can only describe it as unmitigated gall, to try to compare the Government of Canada with the Government of Ontario. He tried to do it in a way that suggested that the Government of Ontario was the one that looked bad, not the Government of Canada. It was, as I say, an unbelievable speech. I thought that he displayed a certain riskiness in making this comparison. I would like to draw on that comparison in a way that is perhaps less favourable than the minister intended.
First, he suggested that the Government of Ontario was somehow less responsible fiscally than the Government of Canada. He suggested that because government spending had increased at a slightly faster rate than this government's had, therefore, somehow it was less responsible.
It is hard to imagine that coming from the minister who, of course, was using figures that could only be described as suspect. He did what the Minister of Finance has done repeatedly in this budget. He draws on figures that show increases in program spending only, not over-all government spending. They somehow think that program spending is different from over-all government spending. Everyone knows that is not so. If the government is short of money at the end of the year, it has to borrow. We have a borrowing bill before this House now. If the government is short of money, it is going to borrow the money and it does not matter whether it was program spending or whether it was to pay interest on the public debt. The fact is the money has to be borrowed from somewhere. This government, with its profligate ways, has run up the national debt in this

The Budget
country to heights unknown before, absolutely astronomical heights.
We sit here and listen to speeches from members on the Conservative side. It sounds as though each speech has been written by officials in the Department of Finance because they all beat the same drum, they all say the same thing over and over and it is silly nonsense. They cite all the deficit figures for the years up to 1984, and then they stop. Why do they stop? They stop because they are so ashamed and embarrassed of the disgraceful record of this government. I see the minister shaking his head. He knows I am right.
Anyway, to go back to the Minister of Supply and Services, he said that the Ontario government had grown excessively while the federal government had cut back. Well, there is a good reason why there has been growth in Toronto in the Ontario government. Ontario has a Liberal government. It has a government with a heart. It does not have a brick for a heart, or a heart of stone. It believes in helping the people that it was elected to serve. It cares for its people. Instead of throwing them out of work, it creates jobs and it is creating them in the Ontario civil service.
Second, Ontario had a budgetary surplus this year. The ministers forget that. This was not a case of a mismanaged economy like this one. The Ontario government generated a surplus this year because it has managed its affairs so prudently. That is the result.
Here we have a record deficit of $30 billion for the fourth year in a row under the Conservatives. It was higher before that. Yet they have predicted $28 billion for four years. They have been wrong every time and the minister will be wrong again this year. Watch it. He will be wrong again, he will be low, and he will be wrong next year.
In 1985 he told us that the deficit this year would be $15 billion. What is it? Double that. How wrong can you be? The man must be mad or something. He has no comprehension of figures. The Treasurer of Ontario knows what he is talking about. He predicted a small deficit. He got a small surplus. That is what you call prudent fiscal management and I wish that the Minister
of Finance would go to Toronto and take some lessons. He needs them.
I want to point out that the surplus of the Ontario government is not on operations; it is over all. It is after paying the interest on the debt of the province of Ontario. This government keeps talking about its operating surplus. That is hogwash. This government has a huge debt, $30 billion of deficit this year, and it keeps talking about an operating surplus. What a lot of poppycock. You do not hear that sort of talk in the Ontario legislature. When they talk about a surplus they talk about a surplus, and they mean surplus, they do not mean this phoney operating surplus that this Minister of Finance spouts about in his budget speeches and illustrates with tables and graphs.
Ontario has a treasurer who knows what he is doing and I suggest that the facts indicate clearly that this government has a Minister of Finance who does not have a clue what he is doing. He is wrong on every prediction he makes. He is wrong on every estimate he has made in every single budget he has introduced. All his figures on interest have been wrong. All his figures on the national debt in every year have been incorrect and every projection he has made for every other year has been wrong.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You keep saying the figures are wrong. What are the figures?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will tell you again. If the member had been here two minutes ago she would have heard me say what the figures were. In 1985 this same Minister of Finance predicted that the national deficit for this year would be $15 billion. It is $30 billion, double what he predicted. What a disaster. I wish the hon. member had been here for the preceding four years to try to help him out. She might have straightened him out, but it might have been the wrong way.
The government of Ontario has been saddled with additional programs because of the cutbacks that have been announced by this government over five years of mismanagement so it has had to hire more people to do the work. This government says it has laid off 11,000 civil servants. The government of Ontario has hired 7,000, according to the Minister of Supply and Services. This government has cut back services to its citizens; the province of Ontario has enhanced its services.
March 6, 1990

What a comparison the Minister of Supply and Services dares to make. And he is a member from Ontario. He must be delighted he lives in a province that is so well managed compared with the way the Government of Canada is mismanaged by the Minister of Finance.
